# How to use this guide

Human Anatomy, Physiology and Pathophysiology I is a new 4-credit course of the PCI B.Pharm 2026 (NEP 2020) scheme. It joins three things that the old scheme taught in separate papers: the structure of the body (anatomy), how it works (physiology) and what goes wrong in disease (pathophysiology). Study one unit at a time: read the notes, redraw every diagram from memory (cell, sarcomere, neuromuscular junction, coagulation cascade, eye, ear, heart, conduction system, ECG), then answer the question bank without looking.

**The five units follow the PCI syllabus exactly** (12 hours each):

| Unit | Normal structure and function | Pathophysiology in the same unit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Body organisation, homeostasis, cell, transport, cell division, junctions, signalling, tissues | Cell injury: causes, mechanisms, adaptations, accumulations, cell death; medical terms |
| 2 | Skin, skeleton, skeletal muscle and its contraction, neuromuscular junction, joints | Psoriasis, dermatitis, leprosy, wound healing, rheumatoid arthritis, osteoporosis, gout |
| 3 | Body fluids, blood, haemopoiesis, haemoglobin, coagulation, blood groups, transfusion, lymphatic system | Inflammation and repair, mediators; iron deficiency, megaloblastic, sickle cell and haemolytic anaemias, thalassaemia, haemophilia |
| 4 | Peripheral and autonomic nervous system, spinal and cranial nerves, eye, ear, nose, tongue | Glaucoma, cataract, myopia, otitis externa, otitis media, vertigo, anosmia |
| 5 | Heart, circulation, vessels, conduction system, cardiac cycle, cardiac output, blood pressure, pulse, ECG | Hypertension, arrhythmias, heart failure, angina, myocardial infarction, atherosclerosis |

Pathophysiology here is taught at the level of cause (aetiology), mechanism (pathogenesis) and clinical features. Drug treatment is studied in pharmacology later, so these notes mention drugs only where they cause or reveal a disease.

**End-semester paper (PCI Table XV, 60 marks, 3 hours).** Sessional (internal) assessment carries a further 40 marks. Confirm the exact paper with your university.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | 20 multiple-choice questions, all compulsory | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Short answers — attempt 5 of 7 | 5 × 4 = 20 |
| C | Long answers — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |

The app's full mock paper follows this pattern. A 20-question, 20-minute quick MCQ test is also included. The question bank has 10-mark long answers, 4-mark short answers and a few 2-mark very short answers for quick recall.

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — a standard question that appears again and again in anatomy, physiology and pathophysiology papers; prepare the full answer with a diagram.
- **Medium** — asked every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — less common, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

The ratings are estimates from syllabus weight and how often similar questions appeared in the old-scheme PCI papers on these topics. This is a new syllabus with no past papers yet, so treat them as a guide, not a promise.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Cell structure and organelles, membrane transport, homeostasis and feedback, epithelial tissue, cell injury mechanisms, adaptations, necrosis vs apoptosis |
| 2 | Skin structure and functions, muscle contraction, neuromuscular junction, classification of joints, rheumatoid arthritis, gout, osteoporosis, wound healing |
| 3 | Composition and functions of blood, haemopoiesis, coagulation cascade, blood groups and Rh, lymph, acute inflammation and mediators, anaemias |
| 4 | Sympathetic vs parasympathetic, cranial nerves table, structure of eye and ear, glaucoma, cataract, otitis media |
| 5 | Conduction system, cardiac cycle, cardiac output, regulation of blood pressure, ECG, hypertension, heart failure, MI and atherosclerosis |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. Every long answer should have a labelled diagram. Draw it neatly in pencil and label at least six parts.
2. For a disease, write in this order: definition → aetiology (causes and risk factors) → pathogenesis (as a flow chart with arrows) → clinical features → complications. This matches how examiners mark pathophysiology.
3. Use comparison tables: necrosis vs apoptosis, acute vs chronic inflammation, sympathetic vs parasympathetic, artery vs vein, angina vs MI, left vs right heart failure, B12 vs folate deficiency.
4. Learn the standard numbers: 206 bones, 31 pairs of spinal nerves, 12 pairs of cranial nerves, blood pH 7.35–7.45, red cell life 120 days, cardiac output about 5 L/min, cardiac cycle 0.8 s, normal BP 120/80 mm Hg, PR interval 0.12–0.20 s.
5. For short (4-mark) answers, give a one-line definition, three or four clear points or a small table, and a mini-diagram if it helps. Do not write a whole page.
6. Learn the clotting factor list with names and the cranial nerve table with type and function; they are favourite short questions and MCQs.
7. Revise the "Remember" list at the end of each unit and the revision sheet the night before the exam.

# Last-night revision sheet

## Unit 1: Body, cells, tissues, cell injury

- Anatomy = structure; physiology = function; pathophysiology = disordered function. Aetiology = cause; pathogenesis = mechanism.
- Levels: chemical → cellular → tissue → organ → system → organism. 11 body systems.
- Homeostasis by feedback: receptor → control centre → effector. Negative (BP, glucose, temperature) restores; positive (labour, clotting) amplifies.
- Organelles: mitochondria (ATP), rough ER (proteins), smooth ER (lipids, drug metabolism), Golgi (packaging), lysosomes (digestion), nucleus (DNA).
- Transport: passive (diffusion, facilitated, osmosis, filtration); active (Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase 3 out/2 in; secondary symport/antiport); vesicular (endocytosis, exocytosis). 0.9% NaCl isotonic.
- Mitosis PMAT → 2 diploid cells; meiosis → 4 haploid gametes.
- Junctions: tight (seal), desmosome (anchor), gap (communication).
- Signalling: contact-dependent, paracrine, synaptic, endocrine.
- Tissues: epithelial (squamous, cuboidal, columnar, stratified, transitional), connective, muscular (skeletal, cardiac, smooth), nervous.
- Injury causes: hypoxia/ischaemia, physical, chemical, infection, immune, genetic, nutritional.
- Mechanisms: membrane damage (free radicals, Ca²⁺), mitochondria (ATP falls, pump fails), ribosomes (less protein → fatty change), nucleus (DNA damage).
- Adaptations: atrophy, hypertrophy, hyperplasia, metaplasia (bronchi in smokers), dysplasia (pre-cancerous).
- Cell swelling = earliest reversible change. Necrosis (groups, swelling, inflammation) vs apoptosis (single cells, shrinkage, no inflammation).

## Unit 2: Skin, bones, muscle, joints

- Epidermis layers (deep → surface): basale, spinosum, granulosum, lucidum, corneum. Dermis has glands, vessels, nerves.
- Skin functions: protection, temperature, sensation, vitamin D, excretion, absorption.
- Psoriasis: IL-23/Th17, TNF → fast turnover, silvery plaques, Auspitz sign, Koebner.
- Dermatitis: atopic (barrier + Th2), irritant (direct damage), allergic contact (type IV, nickel).
- Leprosy: *M. leprae*, skin + Schwann cells; tuberculoid (strong CMI, few bacilli) vs lepromatous (weak CMI, many).
- Wound healing: haemostasis → inflammation → proliferation (granulation tissue) → remodelling; first vs second intention.
- 206 bones: axial 80, appendicular 126. Vertebrae 7C 12T 5L 5S 4Co. Ribs: 7 true, 3 false, 2 floating.
- Sarcomere: Z to Z; contraction: Ca²⁺ → troponin → tropomyosin moves → cross-bridges → power stroke; ATP to detach.
- NMJ: ACh on nicotinic receptors; acetylcholinesterase ends it; myasthenia gravis attacks receptors.
- Joints: fibrous, cartilaginous, synovial (hinge, pivot, ball and socket, saddle, condyloid, plane).
- RA: autoimmune, pannus, symmetrical small joints, RF and anti-CCP. Osteoporosis: resorption > formation, oestrogen loss, fractures. Gout: urate crystals, IL-1β, big toe.

## Unit 3: Blood, lymph, inflammation, anaemias

- Body water 60%: ICF 2/3, ECF 1/3. Blood 5–6 L, plasma 55%, pH 7.35–7.45.
- RBC 4.5–5.5 million/µL, life 120 days; WBC 4,000–11,000/µL; platelets 1.5–4 lakh/µL.
- Haemopoiesis in red marrow; erythropoietin from kidney; needs iron, B12, folate.
- Hb = 4 globins + 4 haem (Fe²⁺); HbA α2β2; haem → biliverdin → bilirubin.
- Coagulation: extrinsic (III, VII; PT) + intrinsic (XII, XI, IX, VIII; aPTT) → X → Xa + Va → thrombin → fibrin → XIII stabilises. Vitamin K: II, VII, IX, X.
- ABO: O donor, AB recipient. Rh: anti-D prevents haemolytic disease of newborn.
- Lymph: 3 L/day; thoracic duct → left subclavian vein. Organs: marrow, thymus, nodes, spleen, MALT.
- Acute inflammation: vasodilatation, permeability → exudate; margination, rolling, adhesion, diapedesis, chemotaxis, phagocytosis.
- Mediators: histamine, 5-HT, prostaglandins (COX), leukotrienes (LOX), bradykinin, complement (C3a, C5a, C3b), cytokines (IL-1, TNF), NO.
- Iron deficiency: microcytic, koilonychia, low ferritin. B12/folate: megaloblasts, macrocytes; B12 also nerve damage.
- Sickle cell: Glu → Val at β6, HbS polymerises → haemolysis + vaso-occlusion.
- Thalassaemia: reduced globin chains; β-major → severe anaemia, marrow expansion, iron overload.
- Haemolytic: hereditary (spherocytosis, G6PD) vs acquired (autoimmune, malaria). Haemophilia A (VIII), B (IX), X-linked, aPTT prolonged, haemarthrosis.

## Unit 4: PNS and special senses

- Sympathetic T1–L2, short pre/long post, NA on α/β; parasympathetic cranial III, VII, IX, X + S2–S4, long pre/short post, ACh on M.
- Spinal nerves 31 pairs (8C 12T 5L 5S 1Co); dorsal root sensory, ventral root motor; plexuses cervical, brachial, lumbar, sacral.
- Cranial nerves: I olfactory, II optic, III oculomotor, IV trochlear, V trigeminal, VI abducens, VII facial, VIII vestibulocochlear, IX glossopharyngeal, X vagus, XI accessory, XII hypoglossal.
- Eye: cornea, sclera, choroid, ciliary body, iris, lens, retina (rods, cones, fovea), aqueous and vitreous humour.
- Ear: external, middle (ossicles, Eustachian tube), inner (cochlea for hearing; vestibule and semicircular canals for balance).
- Smell: olfactory epithelium → olfactory bulb. Taste: VII anterior 2/3, IX posterior 1/3; five tastes.
- Glaucoma: blocked aqueous outflow → raised IOP → optic nerve cupping; open-angle (silent) vs angle-closure (painful emergency).
- Cataract: lens opacity; crystallin aggregation, sorbitol in diabetes.
- Myopia: long eyeball, focus in front of retina, concave lens.
- Otitis externa: canal, Pseudomonas, swimmer's ear. Otitis media: Eustachian tube block in children, bulging drum.
- Vertigo: BPPV, Ménière's, vestibular neuritis. Anosmia: conductive vs sensorineural.

## Unit 5: Cardiovascular system

- Heart: 4 chambers, valves tricuspid, mitral, pulmonary, aortic; chordae tendineae; coronary flow in diastole.
- Conduction: SA node (60–100/min) → AV node (delay) → bundle of His → branches → Purkinje.
- Cardiac cycle 0.8 s; SV 70 mL; EF 55–70%; CO = SV × HR ≈ 5 L/min; Frank–Starling.
- BP = CO × TPR; normal 120/80; baroreceptor reflex (IX, X); RAAS; ADH; ANP.
- ECG: P atrial depolarisation, QRS ventricular depolarisation, T ventricular repolarisation; PR 0.12–0.20 s.
- Hypertension: ≥140/90; 90–95% essential; kidney, sympathetic, RAAS, endothelium; target organs.
- Arrhythmias: abnormal automaticity, triggered activity, re-entry, block; AF → stroke; VF → death.
- Heart failure: sympathetic + RAAS + remodelling (vicious cycle); left → pulmonary oedema, orthopnoea; right → oedema, raised JVP, liver.
- Atherosclerosis: endothelial injury → oxidised LDL → foam cells → fatty streak → fibrous plaque → rupture → thrombus.
- Angina: temporary ischaemia, relieved by rest; MI: necrosis, pain > 30 min, ST elevation, raised troponin.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: the cell is the smallest structural and functional unit of life; it has a plasma membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus.
2. Diagram: cell with plasma membrane, nucleus with nucleolus and nuclear pores, rough and smooth ER, Golgi apparatus, mitochondria, lysosomes, ribosomes, centrosome, cytoskeleton.
3. Plasma membrane: fluid mosaic model of a phospholipid bilayer with cholesterol, integral and peripheral proteins and glycocalyx; selective barrier, transport, receptors, cell identity.
4. Cytosol and cytoskeleton (microfilaments, intermediate filaments, microtubules): site of glycolysis; shape and movement.
5. Ribosomes: protein synthesis; free ribosomes for cytosolic proteins, bound ribosomes for secreted and membrane proteins.
6. Rough ER: synthesis of secretory and membrane proteins. Smooth ER: lipid and steroid synthesis, drug detoxification (cytochrome P450), calcium store in muscle.
7. Golgi apparatus: modifies, sorts and packages proteins into secretory vesicles and lysosomes.
8. Lysosomes: acid hydrolases digest worn-out organelles and engulfed material. Peroxisomes: fatty acid oxidation, catalase destroys H2O2.
9. Mitochondria: double membrane with cristae; aerobic respiration and ATP production; own DNA; release cytochrome c in apoptosis.
10. Centrosome (spindle formation), cilia and flagella (movement).
11. Nucleus: nuclear envelope with pores, chromatin (DNA + histones) carries genes and controls cell activity; nucleolus makes ribosomal RNA.
questions.question: Describe the structure of a typical human cell with a labelled diagram. Give the functions of its organelles.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: cell injury is the set of changes that occur when a cell is exposed to a stress beyond its ability to adapt; it may be reversible or irreversible, ending in cell death.
2. Causes: hypoxia and ischaemia (commonest; anaemia, MI); physical agents (trauma, heat, cold, radiation, electricity); chemicals and drugs (poisons, alcohol, drug overdose); infectious agents (viruses, bacteria, toxins); immunological reactions (autoimmunity, anaphylaxis); genetic defects (sickle cell disease); nutritional imbalance (deficiency or excess); ageing.
3. ATP depletion: mitochondrial damage → less ATP → Na+/K+ pump fails → Na+ and water enter (swelling); anaerobic glycolysis → lactic acid → low pH.
4. Mitochondrial damage: Ca2+ overload, hypoxia and toxins open the permeability transition pore; ATP falls; cytochrome c release starts apoptosis.
5. Influx of calcium: activates phospholipases (membrane breakdown), proteases, endonucleases and ATPases.
6. Free radicals (reactive oxygen species): lipid peroxidation of membranes, protein oxidation, DNA damage.
7. Membrane damage: loss of permeability, leakage of enzymes, lysosomal enzymes released and digest the cell.
8. Ribosome damage: ribosomes detach from rough ER → less protein synthesis → lipid accumulates (fatty change).
9. Nuclear (DNA) damage: unrepaired damage triggers apoptosis; necrotic nucleus shows pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis.
10. Flow chart: injurious agent → biochemical change → reversible injury (swelling, fatty change) → irreversible injury → necrosis or apoptosis.
questions.question: Define cell injury. Describe the causes and the mechanisms (pathogenesis) of cell injury.

questions.answer:
1. Four basic tissues: epithelial, connective, muscular, nervous.
2. General features of epithelium: closely packed cells, little matrix, free apical surface, basement membrane, avascular, high regenerative power.
3. Simple squamous: one layer of flat cells; alveoli, endothelium, mesothelium; diffusion and filtration.
4. Simple cuboidal: kidney tubules, thyroid follicles, ducts; secretion and absorption.
5. Simple columnar (with microvilli and goblet cells): stomach and intestine; absorption and mucus secretion. Ciliated columnar: uterine tubes.
6. Pseudostratified ciliated columnar: trachea and bronchi; traps and moves mucus.
7. Stratified squamous: keratinised in epidermis, non-keratinised in mouth, oesophagus, vagina; protection against abrasion.
8. Transitional epithelium: urinary bladder and ureter; allows stretching.
9. Glandular epithelium: exocrine with ducts (sweat, salivary) and endocrine without ducts (thyroid).
10. Functions: protection, absorption, secretion, excretion, filtration, sensation.
11. Diagrams of squamous, cuboidal, columnar and stratified types.
questions.question: Classify tissues. Describe the structure, location and functions of epithelial tissue with examples.

questions.answer:
1. Homeostasis: maintenance of a stable internal environment despite external change (temperature, pH 7.35–7.45, glucose, BP).
2. Components: controlled condition, receptor (detects change), control centre (compares with set point), effector (produces response).
3. Negative feedback reverses the change: rise in BP → baroreceptors → medulla → heart slows, vessels dilate → BP falls.
4. Positive feedback amplifies: oxytocin and uterine contractions in labour, clotting.
questions.question: Explain homeostasis and the components of a feedback system with an example.

questions.answer:
1. Nature: necrosis is always pathological; apoptosis is programmed, physiological or pathological.
2. Extent: necrosis affects groups of cells; apoptosis single cells.
3. Cell size: swelling in necrosis; shrinkage in apoptosis.
4. Membrane: ruptures in necrosis (contents leak); intact in apoptosis, apoptotic bodies formed.
5. Nucleus: pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis vs chromatin condensation and fragmentation.
6. Inflammation present in necrosis; absent in apoptosis.
7. Examples: myocardial infarction vs endometrial shedding, removal of self-reactive lymphocytes.
questions.question: Differentiate between necrosis and apoptosis.

questions.answer:
1. Atrophy: decrease in cell size; uterus after delivery; limb muscles in a plaster cast.
2. Hypertrophy: increase in cell size; skeletal muscle of athletes, uterus in pregnancy; left ventricle in hypertension.
3. Hyperplasia: increase in cell number; breast at puberty, liver regeneration; endometrial hyperplasia, benign prostatic hyperplasia.
4. Metaplasia: one adult cell type replaced by another better able to stand stress; bronchial columnar to squamous epithelium in smokers, Barrett's oesophagus.
5. Dysplasia (add): disordered growth, pre-cancerous.
questions.question: Define atrophy, hypertrophy, hyperplasia and metaplasia with examples.

questions.answer:
1. Simple diffusion: down a gradient through the lipid bilayer (O2, CO2, lipid-soluble drugs).
2. Facilitated diffusion: down a gradient via carriers or channels; saturable (glucose by GLUT).
3. Osmosis (water) and filtration (pressure-driven, glomerulus).
4. Primary active transport: ATP-driven pump against gradient (Na+/K+-ATPase: 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in).
5. Secondary active transport: uses Na+ gradient; symport (Na+–glucose) and antiport (Na+/Ca2+).
6. Vesicular: endocytosis (phagocytosis, pinocytosis, receptor-mediated) and exocytosis.
questions.question: Describe the types of transport across the cell membrane.

questions.answer:
1. Cells communicate by signal molecules that bind receptors and start signal transduction.
2. Contact-dependent: signal stays on the cell surface and binds a receptor on a touching cell (immune cell recognition).
3. Paracrine: local mediator acts on nearby cells (histamine, prostaglandins, growth factors); autocrine acts on the same cell.
4. Synaptic: neurotransmitter crosses a synapse (acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction); fast and precise.
5. Endocrine: hormone travels in blood to distant cells (insulin, thyroxine); slower, widespread.
questions.question: Explain the forms of intracellular signalling with examples.

questions.answer: Metaplasia is a reversible change in which one adult cell type is replaced by another better able to withstand stress, e.g. ciliated columnar epithelium of the bronchi changing to squamous epithelium in smokers.
questions.question: What is metaplasia? Give one example.

questions.answer: Aetiology is the cause of a disease. Pathogenesis is the sequence of events by which the cause produces the disease.
questions.question: Define aetiology and pathogenesis.

questions.answer:
1. Skin: largest organ; epidermis, dermis, on hypodermis.
2. Epidermis: keratinised stratified squamous, avascular; layers from deep: stratum basale (dividing cells, melanocytes), spinosum (Langerhans cells), granulosum, lucidum (thick skin), corneum (dead keratinised cells).
3. Cells: keratinocytes, melanocytes, Langerhans cells, Merkel cells.
4. Dermis: papillary layer (capillaries, Meissner corpuscles) and reticular layer (collagen, hair follicles, sebaceous and sweat glands, Pacinian corpuscles).
5. Diagram of skin section with layers and appendages.
6. Functions: protection, temperature regulation (sweating, vasomotor changes), sensation, vitamin D synthesis, excretion, immunity, absorption (transdermal drugs), blood reservoir.
7. Wound healing phases: haemostasis → inflammation (neutrophils, macrophages) → proliferation (granulation tissue, collagen, epithelialisation, contraction) → remodelling.
8. First intention (clean incision, thin scar) vs second intention (large gaping wound, much granulation tissue, contraction).
9. Factors delaying healing: infection, poor blood supply, foreign body, diabetes, malnutrition, corticosteroids, old age.
questions.question: Describe the structure and functions of skin with a labelled diagram. Add a note on wound healing.

questions.answer:
1. Organisation: muscle (epimysium) → fascicles (perimysium) → fibres (endomysium) → myofibrils → myofilaments (actin, myosin).
2. Sarcolemma, T tubules, sarcoplasmic reticulum (Ca2+ store), triad.
3. Sarcomere: Z line to Z line; A band (myosin), I band (actin), H zone, M line; diagram.
4. Excitation: ACh released at NMJ → end-plate potential → muscle action potential along sarcolemma and T tubules.
5. Ca2+ released from sarcoplasmic reticulum → binds troponin C → tropomyosin shifts → binding sites on actin exposed.
6. Cross-bridge cycle: energised myosin binds actin → power stroke pulls thin filaments → ATP binds, head detaches → ATP hydrolysed, head re-cocked.
7. Sliding filament theory: I band and H zone shorten, A band constant.
8. Relaxation: ACh destroyed by acetylcholinesterase; Ca2+ pumped back by Ca2+-ATPase.
9. NMJ: axon terminal, synaptic vesicles with ACh, synaptic cleft, motor end plate with nicotinic receptors; Ca2+ entry triggers ACh release; diagram.
10. Clinical note: myasthenia gravis, botulinum toxin, neuromuscular blockers.
questions.question: Describe the structure of skeletal muscle and explain the mechanism of muscle contraction. Add a note on the neuromuscular junction.

questions.answer:
Rheumatoid arthritis
1. Chronic autoimmune symmetrical polyarthritis of small joints.
2. Aetiology: HLA-DR4, female sex, smoking, possible infections; rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP antibodies.
3. Pathogenesis: loss of tolerance → CD4 T cells, B cells, autoantibodies → TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6 → synovitis → pannus erodes cartilage and bone → deformity and ankylosis.
4. Features: morning stiffness over 1 hour, swollen MCP and PIP joints, ulnar deviation, swan-neck, nodules, anaemia, fatigue.
Gout
5. Hyperuricaemia with urate crystal deposition.
6. Aetiology: overproduction (purine-rich diet, alcohol, cell breakdown) or under-excretion (kidney disease, thiazides, low-dose aspirin); male sex, obesity.
7. Pathogenesis: supersaturation → monosodium urate crystals in joints → phagocytosed → NLRP3 inflammasome → IL-1β → acute inflammation; chronic: tophi, kidney stones.
8. Features: sudden severe pain, redness and swelling of first MTP joint (podagra), often at night; needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals.
questions.question: Describe the aetiology, pathogenesis and clinical features of rheumatoid arthritis and gout.

questions.answer:
1. Chronic immune-mediated skin disease with silvery scaly plaques.
2. Triggers: genetic tendency, streptococcal infection, trauma (Koebner), stress, drugs (lithium, beta blockers).
3. Pathogenesis: dendritic cells → IL-12, IL-23 → Th1 and Th17 → TNF-α, IL-17 → keratinocyte proliferation; turnover falls to a few days; parakeratosis, dilated capillaries.
4. Features: well-defined red plaques with silvery scales on elbows, knees, scalp; Auspitz sign; nail pitting; psoriatic arthritis.
questions.question: Describe the pathogenesis and clinical features of psoriasis.

questions.answer:
1. Low bone mass with weak microarchitecture; bone is normally mineralised but reduced.
2. Causes: postmenopausal oestrogen loss, ageing, corticosteroids, hyperthyroidism, immobility, low calcium/vitamin D, smoking, alcohol.
3. Mechanism: resorption by osteoclasts exceeds formation; oestrogen loss raises RANKL and cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF) → more osteoclasts; ageing reduces osteoblast activity.
4. Features: silent until fracture; vertebral collapse (kyphosis, height loss), neck of femur, Colles' fracture; diagnosis by DEXA (T-score ≤ −2.5).
questions.question: Write the pathophysiology of osteoporosis.

questions.answer:
1. Chronic infection by Mycobacterium leprae, acid-fast, slow-growing, prefers cooler parts; droplet spread after long contact.
2. Bacilli enter Schwann cells and macrophages; outcome depends on cell-mediated immunity.
3. Tuberculoid: strong immunity, few bacilli, few hypopigmented anaesthetic patches, thickened nerves, lepromin positive.
4. Lepromatous: weak immunity, many bacilli, symmetrical nodules, leonine face, glove-and-stocking anaesthesia, lepromin negative.
5. Nerve damage → painless injuries, ulcers, deformities (claw hand, foot drop).
questions.question: Give the pathophysiology of leprosy.

questions.answer:
1. Functional: synarthrosis (immovable; sutures), amphiarthrosis (slightly movable; intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis), diarthrosis (freely movable; synovial joints).
2. Structural: fibrous (sutures, syndesmosis, gomphosis), cartilaginous (synchondrosis, symphysis), synovial.
3. Synovial types: plane (intercarpal), hinge (elbow, knee), pivot (atlantoaxial), condyloid (wrist), saddle (thumb CMC), ball and socket (shoulder, hip).
4. Parts of a synovial joint: articular cartilage, capsule, synovial membrane and fluid, ligaments.
questions.question: Classify joints structurally and functionally with examples.

questions.answer:
1. Dermatitis: skin inflammation with itching, redness, vesicles, oozing (acute) or lichenification (chronic).
2. Atopic: inherited allergy tendency, filaggrin barrier defect, Th2 and IgE; flexures in children.
3. Irritant contact: direct damage by detergents, solvents, acids; no immunity needed.
4. Allergic contact: type IV hypersensitivity to nickel, chromium, rubber, hair dye; appears 24–72 h after contact.
5. Seborrhoeic (Malassezia, scalp and face) and photodermatitis.
questions.question: Describe the types of dermatitis and their causes.

questions.answer: The adult skeleton has 206 bones: the axial skeleton (skull, hyoid, ear ossicles, vertebral column, thoracic cage) has 80 and the appendicular skeleton (girdles and limbs) has 126.

questions.answer: In psoriasis, new skin lesions appearing at the site of injury to the skin (a scratch, cut or burn) is called the Koebner phenomenon.
questions.question: What is the Koebner phenomenon?

questions.answer:
1. Haemostasis: vascular spasm, platelet plug, coagulation, fibrinolysis.
2. Clotting factors: I fibrinogen, II prothrombin, III tissue factor, IV calcium, V labile factor, VII stable factor, VIII antihaemophilic factor, IX Christmas factor, X Stuart–Prower factor, XI PTA, XII Hageman factor, XIII fibrin-stabilising factor (no VI).
3. Extrinsic pathway: tissue factor (III) + VII → VIIa → activates X; fast; tested by PT.
4. Intrinsic pathway: contact with collagen → XII → XIIa → XI → XIa → IX → IXa + VIIIa + Ca2+ + phospholipid → activates X; tested by aPTT.
5. Common pathway: Xa + Va + Ca2+ + phospholipid (prothrombinase) → prothrombin → thrombin.
6. Thrombin → fibrinogen to fibrin; XIIIa cross-links fibrin; thrombin also activates V, VIII, XI, XIII and platelets.
7. Flow chart of both pathways meeting at X.
8. Vitamin K-dependent factors II, VII, IX, X (made in liver).
9. Natural anticoagulants: antithrombin III, protein C and S, prostacyclin. Fibrinolysis: plasminogen → plasmin by tPA.
questions.question: Describe the mechanism of blood coagulation with a neat flow chart. Name the clotting factors.

questions.answer:
1. Definition: protective response of vascularised tissue to injury to remove the cause and dead tissue and start repair.
2. Cardinal signs: rubor, tumor, calor, dolor, functio laesa.
3. Classification: acute (neutrophils, short) vs chronic (lymphocytes, macrophages, fibrosis); granulomatous (TB, leprosy).
4. Vascular events: transient vasoconstriction → vasodilatation (redness, heat) → increased permeability (endothelial gaps) → protein-rich exudate (swelling) → stasis.
5. Cellular events: margination → rolling (selectins) → adhesion (integrins, ICAM-1) → diapedesis → chemotaxis (C5a, LTB4, IL-8, bacterial products) → phagocytosis (opsonins IgG, C3b; killing by oxygen radicals and lysosomal enzymes).
6. Mediators: histamine and serotonin (permeability); prostaglandins (vasodilatation, pain, fever); leukotrienes (chemotaxis, bronchoconstriction); PAF; bradykinin (pain, permeability); complement C3a, C5a, C3b, MAC; cytokines IL-1, TNF-α, IL-6, IL-8; nitric oxide.
7. Arachidonic acid pathway diagram: COX → prostaglandins, thromboxane; LOX → leukotrienes.
8. Outcomes: resolution, fibrosis, abscess, chronic inflammation; systemic effects fever, leucocytosis, CRP.
questions.question: Define inflammation. Describe the vascular and cellular events of acute inflammation and list the chemical mediators.

questions.answer:
1. Anaemia: haemoglobin below normal for age and sex. Morphological classification: microcytic hypochromic (iron deficiency, thalassaemia), normocytic (blood loss, haemolysis, chronic disease), macrocytic (B12, folate).
2. Common features: fatigue, pallor, breathlessness, palpitations, tachycardia.
Iron deficiency
3. Causes: low intake, increased need (pregnancy, growth), poor absorption (achlorhydria, coeliac), chronic blood loss (menorrhagia, hookworm, ulcer, piles, NSAIDs).
4. Pathogenesis: ferritin stores depleted → serum iron and transferrin saturation fall, TIBC rises → less haem → microcytic hypochromic cells.
5. Features: koilonychia, angular stomatitis, glossitis, pica, Plummer–Vinson syndrome; low ferritin.
Megaloblastic
6. B12 and folate needed for DNA (thymidine) synthesis; deficiency → nuclear–cytoplasmic asynchrony → megaloblasts, ineffective erythropoiesis → macrocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils.
7. B12 causes: pernicious anaemia (no intrinsic factor), gastrectomy, ileal disease, vegan diet; neurological damage (subacute combined degeneration).
8. Folate causes: poor diet, alcohol, pregnancy, malabsorption, methotrexate, phenytoin; no nerve damage.
questions.question: Classify anaemias. Describe the aetiology and pathogenesis of iron deficiency anaemia and megaloblastic anaemia.

questions.answer:
1. ABO: antigens A and B on red cells, natural antibodies in plasma against the absent antigen; groups A, B, AB (universal recipient), O (universal donor).
2. Rh: D antigen present in most Indians; anti-D formed only after exposure.
3. HDN: Rh-negative mother sensitised by Rh-positive fetus at delivery → anti-D IgG crosses placenta in next Rh-positive pregnancy → fetal haemolysis, jaundice, hydrops.
4. Prevention: anti-D immunoglobulin to the mother after delivery.
questions.question: Explain the ABO and Rh blood group systems. Add a note on haemolytic disease of the newborn.

questions.answer:
1. Formation of blood cells; yolk sac → liver and spleen → bone marrow; adult red marrow of flat bones and ends of long bones.
2. Pluripotent stem cell → myeloid and lymphoid stem cells.
3. Myeloid → proerythroblast → normoblasts → reticulocyte → RBC; myeloblast → granulocytes; monoblast → monocyte; megakaryoblast → megakaryocyte → platelets. Lymphoid → B and T lymphocytes.
4. Control: erythropoietin (kidney), colony-stimulating factors, thrombopoietin; needs iron, B12, folate, protein.
questions.question: Describe haemopoiesis with a flow chart.

questions.answer:
1. Autosomal recessive; valine replaces glutamic acid at position 6 of β-globin → HbS.
2. Deoxygenated HbS polymerises → rigid sickle cells; triggers low O2, dehydration, acidosis, infection.
3. Haemolysis: red cell life 10–20 days → anaemia, jaundice, gallstones.
4. Vaso-occlusion: painful crises, bone, lung (acute chest), spleen infarcts (autosplenectomy, infections), stroke.
5. Trait (HbAS) usually symptom-free, some protection against malaria.
questions.question: Describe the pathogenesis of sickle cell anaemia.

questions.answer:
1. About 3 L of filtered fluid not reabsorbed by capillaries enters blind lymphatic capillaries (overlapping endothelial flaps) → lymph; chyle from lacteals.
2. Circulation: capillaries → vessels with valves → nodes → trunks → thoracic duct (to left subclavian vein) and right lymphatic duct (to right subclavian vein).
3. Driven by muscle pump, respiratory pump, vessel smooth muscle, valves.
4. Functions: returns fluid and protein (prevents oedema), fat absorption, immune defence.
questions.question: Describe the formation, circulation and functions of lymph.

questions.answer:
1. Inherited bleeding disorder: haemophilia A (factor VIII, commonest), haemophilia B (factor IX).
2. X-linked recessive: males affected, females carriers.
3. Lack of VIII or IX blocks intrinsic pathway (tenase) → slow thrombin and fibrin formation → unstable clot.
4. Features: haemarthrosis, muscle bleeds, prolonged bleeding after injury or extraction; aPTT prolonged, PT and bleeding time normal.
questions.question: Write the aetiology and pathogenesis of haemophilia.

questions.answer: Factors II (prothrombin), VII, IX and X are vitamin K-dependent; they are made in the liver.
questions.question: Name the vitamin K-dependent clotting factors.

questions.answer: Thalassaemia is an inherited (autosomal recessive) disorder with reduced or absent synthesis of α or β globin chains, causing microcytic hypochromic anaemia with haemolysis and ineffective erythropoiesis.
questions.question: What is thalassaemia?

questions.answer:
1. ANS: two-neuron efferent system to heart, smooth muscle, glands; preganglionic (myelinated) and postganglionic (unmyelinated) neurons.
2. Origin: sympathetic thoracolumbar T1–L2 (lateral horn); parasympathetic craniosacral (III, VII, IX, X; S2–S4).
3. Ganglia: sympathetic chain and prevertebral ganglia near cord (short pre, long post); parasympathetic near or in organs (long pre, short post).
4. Transmitters: ACh at all ganglia (nicotinic); sympathetic postganglionic noradrenaline (α, β) except ACh at sweat glands; parasympathetic ACh (muscarinic). Adrenal medulla releases adrenaline.
5. Divergence: sympathetic widespread, parasympathetic localised.
6. Effects table: pupil dilation vs constriction; heart rate up vs down; bronchodilation vs bronchoconstriction; gut motility down vs up; bladder retention vs voiding; glycogenolysis vs glycogenesis; thick vs watery saliva; ejaculation vs erection.
7. Roles: fight or flight vs rest and digest; dual innervation with opposing effects.
8. Diagram of the two-neuron pathways.
questions.question: Compare the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems with respect to origin, ganglia, neurotransmitters and effects on organs.

questions.answer:
1. Diagram: cornea, sclera, choroid, ciliary body, iris, pupil, lens, aqueous and vitreous humour, retina, fovea, optic disc, optic nerve.
2. Coats: fibrous (sclera, cornea), vascular (choroid, ciliary body, iris), nervous (retina with rods and cones).
3. Accessory structures: eyelids, conjunctiva, lacrimal apparatus, extrinsic muscles.
4. Aqueous humour: secreted by ciliary processes → posterior chamber → pupil → anterior chamber → trabecular meshwork → canal of Schlemm.
Glaucoma
5. Optic neuropathy with raised intraocular pressure (above 21 mm Hg) from blocked outflow → optic disc cupping → peripheral field loss first.
6. Open-angle (meshwork resistance, painless, slow) vs angle-closure (iris blocks angle; acute painful red eye, haloes, vomiting; emergency); secondary (steroids) and congenital.
Cataract
7. Lens opacity: ageing (commonest), diabetes, steroids, UV, smoking, trauma, congenital rubella.
8. Oxidation and aggregation of crystallins; in diabetes aldose reductase → sorbitol → osmotic swelling.
9. Features: painless blurring, glare, faded colours, white pupil.
questions.question: Describe the structure of the eye with a labelled diagram. Explain the pathophysiology of glaucoma and cataract.

questions.answer:
1. External ear: auricle, external acoustic meatus with wax glands.
2. Middle ear: tympanic membrane, ossicles (malleus, incus, stapes), Eustachian tube to nasopharynx, oval and round windows.
3. Inner ear: bony labyrinth (perilymph) and membranous labyrinth (endolymph): cochlea with organ of Corti, vestibule (utricle, saccule), three semicircular canals. Diagram.
4. Hearing: sound → eardrum → ossicles amplify → oval window → fluid waves → basilar membrane moves → hair cells bend against tectorial membrane → cochlear nerve → auditory cortex (temporal lobe).
5. Balance: utricle and saccule (static), semicircular canals (rotation).
Otitis media
6. Common in children (short, horizontal Eustachian tube, adenoids); follows upper respiratory infection; S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis.
7. Tube blocked → negative pressure → effusion → infection → pus → bulging drum → may perforate.
8. Features: earache, fever, hearing loss, discharge; complications mastoiditis, meningitis, deafness.
questions.question: Describe the structure of the ear and the physiology of hearing. Write the pathophysiology of otitis media.

questions.answer: I olfactory (S, smell); II optic (S, vision); III oculomotor (M, eye movement, eyelid, pupil constriction); IV trochlear (M, superior oblique); V trigeminal (B, face sensation, chewing); VI abducens (M, lateral rectus); VII facial (B, facial expression, taste anterior 2/3, tears and saliva); VIII vestibulocochlear (S, hearing and balance); IX glossopharyngeal (B, taste posterior 1/3, swallowing, parotid); X vagus (B, parasympathetic to heart, lungs, gut); XI accessory (M, sternocleidomastoid, trapezius); XII hypoglossal (M, tongue).
questions.question: List the cranial nerves with their type and main functions.

questions.answer:
1. 31 pairs: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal.
2. Formed by dorsal root (sensory, with dorsal root ganglion) and ventral root (motor) joining in the intervertebral foramen → mixed nerve.
3. Branches: dorsal ramus (back), ventral ramus (limbs, trunk), meningeal branch, rami communicantes.
4. Plexuses: cervical C1–C4 (phrenic), brachial C5–T1 (radial, median, ulnar), lumbar L1–L4 (femoral), sacral L4–S4 (sciatic); intercostal nerves T2–T12.
5. Dermatomes; functions: sensation, movement, reflexes.
questions.question: Describe the origin and distribution of spinal nerves.

questions.answer:
1. Vertigo: false sense of spinning; symptom of vestibular dysfunction.
2. Balance compares signals from both vestibular organs, eyes and proprioceptors; an abnormal one-sided signal is felt as movement.
3. Peripheral causes: BPPV (loose otoconia in a semicircular canal), Ménière's disease (endolymphatic hydrops with hearing loss and tinnitus), vestibular neuritis, labyrinthitis, aminoglycoside damage.
4. Central causes: stroke, multiple sclerosis, tumours, migraine.
5. Features: spinning, nausea, vomiting, nystagmus, unsteadiness.
questions.question: Explain the pathophysiology of vertigo.

questions.answer:
1. Refractive error: parallel rays focus in front of the retina; distant objects blurred, near clear.
2. Causes: axial (eyeball too long) or refractive (too much corneal or lens power); genetics, near work, little outdoor time.
3. Diagram of focus in front of retina.
4. Corrected by a concave (diverging) lens; high myopia risks retinal detachment and glaucoma.
5. Contrast: hypermetropia (convex lens), presbyopia (loss of accommodation).
questions.question: What is myopia? Explain its cause and correction.

questions.answer:
1. Papillae: circumvallate, fungiform, foliate (have taste buds), filiform (none).
2. Taste bud: gustatory cells with microvilli at a taste pore, supporting and basal cells.
3. Five tastes: sweet, salty, sour, bitter, umami; nerves VII (anterior 2/3), IX (posterior 1/3), X → medulla → thalamus → gustatory cortex.
4. Anosmia: loss of smell; conductive (cold, polyps, sinusitis) or sensorineural (viral infection including COVID-19, head injury, ageing, Parkinson's); affects flavour and safety.
questions.question: Describe the structure of the tongue and the physiology of taste. Add a note on anosmia.

questions.answer: Cranial nerves III (oculomotor), VII (facial), IX (glossopharyngeal) and X (vagus) carry parasympathetic fibres.
questions.question: Name the parasympathetic cranial nerves.

questions.answer: Otitis externa is inflammation of the external ear canal, usually by Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus aureus or fungi, favoured by moisture (swimmer's ear) and injury to the canal skin; pain increases on pulling the pinna.
questions.question: What is otitis externa?

questions.answer:
1. Position in mediastinum; apex at left fifth intercostal space; pericardium (fibrous and serous); wall: epicardium, myocardium, endocardium.
2. Chambers: two atria, two ventricles; septa; left ventricle thickest.
3. Valves: tricuspid, mitral, pulmonary, aortic; chordae tendineae and papillary muscles.
4. Coronary arteries (right, left anterior descending, circumflex); coronary sinus. Diagram with chambers, valves and great vessels.
5. Conduction: SA node (pacemaker 60–100/min) → atria → AV node (0.1 s delay) → bundle of His → bundle branches → Purkinje fibres.
6. Pacemaker potential: funny current, Ca2+ upstroke; ventricular action potential with Ca2+ plateau and long refractory period.
7. Sympathetic (noradrenaline on β1): increases rate, force and conduction velocity.
8. Parasympathetic (vagus, ACh on M2): slows SA rate and AV conduction; vagal tone dominates at rest.
9. Cardiovascular centre in medulla, baroreceptor input; hormones and ions also affect the heart.
questions.question: Describe the anatomy of the heart with a labelled diagram. Explain the conduction system of the heart and its regulation by the autonomic nervous system.

questions.answer:
1. BP: pressure of blood on arterial walls; systolic about 120, diastolic about 80 mm Hg; pulse pressure, mean arterial pressure.
2. BP = cardiac output × total peripheral resistance; CO = SV × HR; resistance depends on radius (fourth power), length, viscosity.
3. Short-term: baroreceptor reflex (carotid sinus IX, aortic arch X → medulla → vagal and sympathetic changes); chemoreceptor reflex.
4. Hormonal: renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system; ADH; ANP; adrenaline.
5. Long-term: renal pressure natriuresis and blood volume.
6. Hypertension: ≥140/90 mm Hg; essential (90–95%) and secondary (renal, endocrine, coarctation, drugs).
7. Pathogenesis: renal Na+ retention, sympathetic overactivity, RAAS, endothelial dysfunction (less NO, more endothelin), insulin resistance → raised CO and resistance → arteriolar thickening.
8. Complications: LVH and heart failure, stroke, nephrosclerosis, retinopathy, atherosclerosis; malignant hypertension.
questions.question: Define blood pressure. Describe the factors and mechanisms that regulate blood pressure. Add a note on the pathophysiology of hypertension.

questions.answer:
1. IHD: myocardial oxygen supply less than demand, mostly due to coronary atherosclerosis.
2. Risk factors: age, male sex, family history; high LDL, low HDL, hypertension, smoking, diabetes, obesity, inactivity.
3. Atherosclerosis: endothelial injury → LDL enters and is oxidised → monocytes become macrophages → foam cells → fatty streak → smooth muscle migration and collagen → fibrous cap over lipid core → plaque; complications: rupture, thrombosis, calcification, aneurysm.
4. Angina: transient ischaemia when demand exceeds supply; stable (exertion, relieved by rest), unstable (plaque rupture with partial thrombus, at rest), variant (spasm).
5. Pain: central chest tightness radiating to left arm, jaw; a few minutes.
6. MI: plaque rupture → platelet aggregation → occlusive thrombus → necrosis after 20–30 min, spreading from subendocardium outward.
7. Features: crushing pain over 30 min not relieved by rest or nitrates, sweating, vomiting, breathlessness.
8. Diagnosis: ST elevation, Q waves; raised troponin, CK-MB.
9. Complications: arrhythmias (VF), heart failure, cardiogenic shock, rupture, aneurysm, thromboembolism, pericarditis.
10. Table: angina vs MI.
questions.question: Describe the pathophysiology of ischaemic heart disease with reference to atherosclerosis, angina pectoris and myocardial infarction.

questions.answer:
1. Events of one heartbeat; 0.8 s at 72/min (atrial systole 0.1 s, ventricular systole 0.3 s, ventricular diastole 0.5 s).
2. Atrial systole: completes ventricular filling.
3. Isovolumetric contraction: AV valves close (first sound), all valves closed.
4. Ejection: semilunar valves open, blood ejected.
5. Isovolumetric relaxation: semilunar valves close (second sound).
6. Ventricular filling: rapid and slow filling. EDV about 120 mL, ESV about 50 mL, SV about 70 mL.
questions.question: Describe the cardiac cycle.

questions.answer:
1. ECG records electrical activity of the heart from skin electrodes (12 leads).
2. P wave: atrial depolarisation.
3. PR interval 0.12–0.20 s: AV nodal delay.
4. QRS complex (under 0.12 s): ventricular depolarisation; atrial repolarisation hidden.
5. ST segment: ventricles depolarised; T wave: ventricular repolarisation; QT about 0.4 s.
6. Uses: rate, rhythm, arrhythmias, blocks, ischaemia and infarction, electrolyte changes.
questions.question: Draw a normal ECG and explain its waves and intervals.

questions.answer:
1. Heart cannot pump enough blood for body needs; causes: IHD, hypertension, valve disease, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmias.
2. Compensation: Frank–Starling, sympathetic activation, RAAS (salt and water retention), ADH, remodelling → short-term help, long-term worsening.
3. Left failure: pulmonary congestion, dyspnoea, orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, crackles.
4. Right failure: raised JVP, pedal oedema, enlarged liver, ascites; commonest cause left failure; cor pulmonale from lung disease.
questions.question: Describe the pathogenesis and features of congestive heart failure.

questions.answer:
1. Volume pumped by each ventricle per minute; CO = SV × HR ≈ 70 mL × 72 = about 5 L/min.
2. Preload (end-diastolic volume, venous return; Frank–Starling law).
3. Contractility (increased by sympathetic stimulation and adrenaline; reduced by hypoxia, acidosis).
4. Afterload (aortic pressure; raised in hypertension).
5. Heart rate (autonomic nerves, hormones, temperature, exercise).
questions.question: Define cardiac output and describe the factors affecting it.

questions.answer:
1. Arrhythmia: abnormal rate, rhythm or conduction.
2. Abnormal automaticity: SA node too fast or slow, ectopic foci (ischaemia, low K+, sympathetic drive).
3. Triggered activity: early after-depolarisations (long QT) and delayed after-depolarisations (Ca2+ overload, digoxin toxicity).
4. Re-entry: impulse circles a loop with one-way block and slow conduction (most tachycardias).
5. Conduction block (AV block).
6. Examples: atrial fibrillation (stroke risk), ventricular fibrillation (cardiac arrest).
questions.question: Explain the mechanisms of cardiac arrhythmias.

questions.answer: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate; at rest about 70 mL × 72 beats/min, which is about 5 L/min.
questions.question: What is the normal cardiac output? Give its formula.

questions.answer: The QRS complex represents depolarisation of the ventricles (atrial repolarisation is hidden within it); it normally lasts less than 0.12 s.

title: Human Anatomy, Physiology and Pathophysiology I

units.markdown:
# Unit 1: Introduction to the human body, cells, tissues, and cell injury and adaptation

This unit lays the foundation for the whole subject. It defines anatomy, physiology and pathophysiology, shows how the body is organised from atoms to systems, explains how the body keeps its internal conditions steady, and then goes down to the cell: its parts, how substances cross its membrane, how it divides and how cells signal to each other. It then covers the four basic tissues. The last part is the first taste of pathophysiology: what injures a cell, how a cell adapts, and how it finally dies.

## 1.1 Definition and scope

| Term | Definition | Examples of branches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Anatomy** | Study of the structure (form) of the body and its parts and how the parts are related | Gross anatomy, histology (tissues), cytology (cells), embryology, surface and radiological anatomy |
| **Physiology** | Study of the normal functions of the body and its parts | Cell physiology, neurophysiology, cardiovascular, renal and endocrine physiology |
| **Pathophysiology** | Study of the disordered functions that cause or follow disease or injury | Cardiovascular, haematological, joint and skin pathophysiology |
| **Pathology** | Study of the structural and functional changes in cells, tissues and organs in disease | General pathology (cell injury, inflammation), systemic pathology (disease of each organ) |

**Scope for a pharmacy student.** Every drug acts on a cell, a tissue or an organ. Pharmacology, pharmacokinetics (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion), dosage-form design, clinical pharmacy and patient counselling all assume a working picture of normal structure and function, and of what goes wrong in disease. For example, a transdermal patch is designed around the layers of skin, an eye drop around the cornea and tear drainage, and an antihypertensive drug around the factors that set blood pressure.

Key words used in pathophysiology:

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Aetiology (etiology) | The cause of a disease |
| Pathogenesis | The sequence of events by which the cause produces the disease |
| Morphological changes | Structural changes in cells and tissues |
| Clinical features | Signs (found by the examiner) and symptoms (felt by the patient) |
| Complications | Further problems that arise from the disease |
| Prognosis | Likely outcome |

## 1.2 Levels of structural organisation and body systems

```text
Chemical level      atoms (C, H, O, N, Ca) -> molecules (water, glucose, proteins, DNA)
      |
Cellular level      cell: smallest unit of life (neuron, muscle fibre, red cell)
      |
Tissue level        group of similar cells with a common job (epithelial, connective,
      |             muscular, nervous)
Organ level         two or more tissues forming a structure of definite shape (heart, skin)
      |
System level        related organs with a common function (cardiovascular system)
      |
Organismal level    the whole person: all systems working together
```

| System | Main organs | Main function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Integumentary | Skin, hair, nails, sweat and sebaceous glands | Protection, temperature control, vitamin D synthesis |
| Skeletal | Bones, cartilage, joints | Support, protection, movement, blood cell formation, mineral store |
| Muscular | Skeletal muscles and tendons | Movement, posture, heat |
| Nervous | Brain, spinal cord, nerves, sense organs | Rapid control by nerve impulses |
| Endocrine | Pituitary, thyroid, adrenal, pancreatic islets, gonads | Slower control by hormones |
| Cardiovascular | Heart, blood vessels, blood | Transport of gases, nutrients, wastes, hormones |
| Lymphatic and immune | Lymph vessels, lymph nodes, spleen, thymus, tonsils | Return of tissue fluid, fat absorption, defence |
| Respiratory | Nose, larynx, trachea, bronchi, lungs | Gas exchange, pH control |
| Digestive | Mouth to anus, liver, gall bladder, pancreas | Digestion and absorption |
| Urinary | Kidneys, ureters, bladder, urethra | Removal of waste, water, electrolyte and pH balance |
| Reproductive | Testes, ovaries, uterus and ducts | Production of offspring |

## 1.3 Basic life processes

1. **Metabolism** – all chemical reactions in the body: catabolism (breakdown, releases energy) and anabolism (synthesis, uses energy).
2. **Responsiveness** – detecting and reacting to changes (a nerve impulse, a gland secreting).
3. **Movement** – of the whole body, of organs (the beating heart), of cells (white cells moving into tissue) and inside cells.
4. **Growth** – increase in size by more cells or larger cells.
5. **Differentiation** – unspecialised cells becoming specialised (stem cells to red cells).
6. **Reproduction** – new cells for growth and repair, and a new individual.

## 1.4 Homeostasis and feedback systems

**Homeostasis** is the maintenance of a relatively stable internal environment (the extracellular fluid around the cells) in spite of changes outside. Variables kept within narrow limits include body temperature (about 37 °C), blood glucose, blood pressure, blood pH (7.35–7.45), oxygen and carbon dioxide levels, and water and electrolyte concentrations. Disease can be seen as a failure of homeostasis.

### Components of a feedback system

```text
Stimulus (change in a controlled condition)
      |
Receptor  -- detects the change, sends input (afferent path) -->
      |
Control centre (usually brain) -- compares with the set point, decides -->
      |
Effector (muscle or gland) -- output (efferent path) produces a response -->
      |
Controlled condition returns towards normal (or is pushed further away)
```

| Component | Example: control of body temperature |
| --- | --- |
| Controlled condition | Body temperature |
| Receptor | Thermoreceptors in skin and hypothalamus |
| Control centre | Hypothalamus (set point about 37 °C) |
| Effector | Sweat glands, skin blood vessels, skeletal muscle (shivering) |

### Types of feedback

| Negative feedback | Positive feedback |
| --- | --- |
| Response **reverses** the original change | Response **strengthens** the original change |
| Keeps conditions stable; the usual type | Must be stopped by an outside event |
| Examples: control of blood pressure by baroreceptors; blood glucose by insulin and glucagon; body temperature | Examples: uterine contractions during labour (oxytocin), blood clotting, milk ejection |

**Homeostatic imbalance.** When feedback fails, disorders arise: fever beyond control, diabetes mellitus (failed glucose control), hypertension (failed pressure control).

## 1.5 Basic anatomical terminology

**Anatomical position:** body erect, facing forward, head level, eyes looking forward, arms at the sides with palms facing forward, feet flat and forward. All directions are described from this position.

| Term | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Superior / inferior | Towards the head / towards the feet | Heart is superior to the diaphragm |
| Anterior (ventral) / posterior (dorsal) | Front / back | Sternum is anterior to the heart |
| Medial / lateral | Nearer / farther from the midline | Ulna is medial to the radius |
| Proximal / distal | Nearer / farther from the attachment of a limb | Elbow is proximal to the wrist |
| Superficial / deep | Towards / away from the surface | Skin is superficial to muscle |
| Ipsilateral / contralateral | Same side / opposite side | |

**Planes:** sagittal (divides into right and left; the midsagittal plane into equal halves), frontal or coronal (anterior and posterior parts), transverse or horizontal (superior and inferior parts), oblique.

**Body cavities:** dorsal cavity (cranial cavity with brain, vertebral canal with spinal cord) and ventral cavity (thoracic cavity with pleural and pericardial cavities and the mediastinum; abdominopelvic cavity), separated by the diaphragm. The abdomen is divided into nine regions (right and left hypochondriac, epigastric, right and left lumbar, umbilical, right and left iliac, hypogastric) or four quadrants.

## 1.6 Structure and functions of the cell

A typical human cell has three main parts: the plasma membrane, the cytoplasm (cytosol plus organelles) and the nucleus.

```text
        ______________ plasma membrane _______________
       /   ribosomes   rough ER        mitochondrion  \
      |       .  .   ========           (  ~~~~  )     |
      |  Golgi   ))))    ( NUCLEUS )                    |
      |  apparatus       ( nucleolus)   lysosome (o)    |
      |                   nuclear envelope with pores   |
      |  smooth ER ~~~~      centrosome ::   cytosol     |
       \_______________________________________________/
```

| Part | Structure | Function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Plasma membrane** | Phospholipid bilayer with cholesterol, integral and peripheral proteins and surface glycocalyx (fluid mosaic model) | Selective barrier, transport, receptors for signals, cell identity, adhesion |
| **Cytosol** | Watery fluid with ions, nutrients, enzymes | Site of glycolysis and many reactions |
| **Cytoskeleton** | Microfilaments, intermediate filaments, microtubules | Shape, movement, transport of organelles |
| **Centrosome** | Pair of centrioles | Organises the mitotic spindle |
| **Cilia and flagella** | Microtubule projections | Move fluid over the cell (respiratory tract) or move the cell (sperm) |
| **Ribosomes** | rRNA and protein; free or on rough ER | Protein synthesis |
| **Rough ER** | Membrane sacs with ribosomes | Makes proteins for secretion and membranes |
| **Smooth ER** | Tubules without ribosomes | Lipid and steroid synthesis, drug detoxification (cytochrome P450 in liver), calcium store in muscle (sarcoplasmic reticulum) |
| **Golgi apparatus** | Stack of flattened sacs | Modifies, sorts and packages proteins into vesicles |
| **Lysosomes** | Vesicles with acid hydrolases | Digest worn-out organelles and engulfed material (autophagy) |
| **Peroxisomes** | Vesicles with oxidases and catalase | Break down fatty acids, destroy hydrogen peroxide |
| **Mitochondria** | Double membrane, inner folds (cristae), own DNA | Aerobic respiration, ATP production ("powerhouse"); trigger apoptosis |
| **Nucleus** | Nuclear envelope with pores, chromatin (DNA + histones), nucleolus | Holds genetic information, controls cell activity; nucleolus makes ribosomes |

## 1.7 Transport across the cell membrane

| Process | Energy | Mechanism | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Simple diffusion** | Passive | Movement down a concentration gradient through the lipid bilayer | O2, CO2, lipid-soluble drugs |
| **Facilitated diffusion** | Passive | Down a gradient with a carrier or channel protein; shows saturation | Glucose into most cells (GLUT carriers) |
| **Osmosis** | Passive | Movement of water across a selectively permeable membrane towards higher solute concentration | Water movement in red cells |
| **Filtration** | Passive (pressure) | Movement of water and small solutes due to hydrostatic pressure | Glomerular filtration, capillary filtration |
| **Primary active transport** | ATP used directly | Carrier pumps against the gradient | Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase: 3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in |
| **Secondary active transport** | Uses the Na⁺ gradient made by the pump | Symport (same direction) or antiport (opposite) | Na⁺–glucose symport in intestine; Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchanger |
| **Endocytosis** | ATP | Membrane folds inward to form vesicles: phagocytosis (cell eating), pinocytosis (cell drinking), receptor-mediated endocytosis | Bacteria by neutrophils; LDL uptake |
| **Exocytosis** | ATP | Vesicles fuse with the membrane and release contents | Neurotransmitter and hormone release |

**Tonicity:** in an isotonic solution (0.9% NaCl) red cells keep their shape; in a hypotonic solution they swell and may burst (haemolysis); in a hypertonic solution they shrink (crenation). This is why injections and eye drops are made isotonic.

## 1.8 Cell division

**Cell cycle:** interphase (G1 growth, S DNA replication, G2 preparation) followed by the mitotic (M) phase.

**Mitosis** gives two identical diploid (46-chromosome) daughter cells; used for growth and repair.

| Stage | Events |
| --- | --- |
| Prophase | Chromatin condenses into chromosomes (two chromatids joined at the centromere); spindle forms; nuclear envelope breaks down |
| Metaphase | Chromosomes line up at the equator (metaphase plate) |
| Anaphase | Centromeres split; sister chromatids pulled to opposite poles |
| Telophase | Nuclear envelopes re-form, chromosomes uncoil |
| Cytokinesis | Cytoplasm divides by a cleavage furrow |

**Meiosis** occurs in the gonads: two divisions give four haploid (23-chromosome) gametes; crossing over in prophase I creates genetic variety.

## 1.9 Cell junctions

| Junction | Structure | Function | Site |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tight junction | Membranes fused by proteins in a band | Seals the gap; stops leakage between cells | Intestine, blood–brain barrier, kidney tubules |
| Adherens junction | Cadherins linked to actin | Holds cells together | Epithelia |
| Desmosome | Spot-like plaque with cadherins and intermediate filaments | Strong attachment against stretching | Skin, heart muscle |
| Hemidesmosome | Half desmosome with integrins | Anchors cells to the basement membrane | Base of epithelium |
| Gap junction | Channels of connexons | Passage of ions and small molecules; electrical coupling | Heart and smooth muscle |

## 1.10 Cell communication and intracellular signalling

Cells coordinate their activity by sending signals (ligands) that bind receptors on or in the target cell. The receptor then starts an internal chain of events (signal transduction) that changes the cell's activity.

| Form | How the signal travels | Distance | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **a) Contact-dependent** | Signal molecule stays on the surface of the sending cell and binds a receptor on a touching cell | Direct contact | Immune cells recognising antigen on other cells; signals that guide development |
| **b) Paracrine** | Local mediator released into tissue fluid acts on nearby cells | Short | Histamine, prostaglandins, growth factors, nitric oxide (autocrine when it acts on the same cell) |
| **c) Synaptic** | Neurotransmitter released at a synapse acts on the next neuron or effector | Very short gap, very fast | Acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction |
| **d) Endocrine** | Hormone released into blood, carried to distant targets | Long, slower | Insulin, thyroxine, adrenaline |

Main receptor types (background for pharmacology): ligand-gated ion channels (nicotinic acetylcholine receptor), G-protein coupled receptors (adrenergic and muscarinic receptors, using cAMP, IP3 and calcium as second messengers), enzyme-linked receptors (insulin receptor tyrosine kinase), and intracellular receptors (steroid and thyroid hormones acting on genes).

## 1.11 Tissues: classification, structure, location and functions

A tissue is a group of similar cells and their surrounding material that perform a common function. There are four basic tissues.

### Epithelial tissue

Closely packed cells, little matrix, a free (apical) surface, resting on a basement membrane, no blood vessels (nourished by diffusion), good power of regeneration.

| Type | Structure | Location | Function |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Simple squamous | One layer of flat cells | Alveoli, lining of blood vessels (endothelium), serous membranes (mesothelium) | Diffusion, filtration |
| Simple cuboidal | One layer of cube-shaped cells | Kidney tubules, thyroid follicles, gland ducts | Secretion, absorption |
| Simple columnar | One layer of tall cells, may have microvilli or goblet cells | Stomach and intestine lining | Absorption, secretion of mucus |
| Ciliated columnar | Columnar with cilia | Uterine tubes | Moves the ovum |
| Pseudostratified ciliated columnar | One layer that looks layered, cilia and goblet cells | Trachea, bronchi | Traps and moves mucus |
| Stratified squamous | Many layers, flat surface cells; keratinised or not | Skin epidermis (keratinised); mouth, oesophagus, vagina (non-keratinised) | Protection against wear |
| Transitional | Layers that change shape when stretched | Urinary bladder, ureters | Allows stretching |
| Glandular | Exocrine (with ducts: sweat, salivary) and endocrine (ductless: thyroid) | Glands | Secretion |

### Connective tissue

Widely spaced cells in an abundant matrix of ground substance and fibres (collagen, elastic, reticular); usually vascular (except cartilage).

| Type | Main features | Location | Function |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Loose (areolar) | Fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells, all three fibres | Under skin, around organs | Binding, support, defence |
| Adipose | Fat cells | Subcutaneous tissue, around kidneys | Energy store, insulation |
| Reticular | Reticular fibres | Spleen, lymph nodes, bone marrow | Framework |
| Dense regular | Parallel collagen bundles | Tendons, ligaments | Strong attachment |
| Dense irregular | Collagen in many directions | Dermis | Strength in all directions |
| Elastic | Elastic fibres | Walls of large arteries | Stretch and recoil |
| Hyaline cartilage | Chondrocytes in lacunae, fine collagen | Articular surfaces, costal cartilage, trachea | Smooth surface, support |
| Fibrocartilage | Thick collagen bundles | Intervertebral discs, menisci, pubic symphysis | Shock absorption |
| Elastic cartilage | Elastic fibres | Ear auricle, epiglottis | Flexible support |
| Bone | Calcified matrix, osteocytes in lacunae, osteons | Skeleton | Support, protection, calcium store |
| Blood | Cells in liquid plasma | Vessels | Transport |

### Muscular tissue

| Feature | Skeletal | Cardiac | Smooth |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Shape | Long cylindrical fibres | Branched cells | Spindle-shaped |
| Nuclei | Many, peripheral | One (or two), central | One, central |
| Striations | Present | Present | Absent |
| Special feature | — | Intercalated discs (gap junctions and desmosomes) | Gap junctions in single-unit type |
| Control | Voluntary | Involuntary, autorhythmic | Involuntary |
| Location | Attached to bones | Heart | Walls of gut, vessels, bladder, uterus |

### Nervous tissue

**Neurons** carry nerve impulses: a cell body (with Nissl bodies), dendrites (receive signals) and one axon (carries impulses away), often covered by a myelin sheath with nodes of Ranvier (faster conduction). **Neuroglia** support neurons: astrocytes (blood–brain barrier support), oligodendrocytes (myelin in the CNS), microglia (phagocytes), ependymal cells (line ventricles), Schwann cells (myelin in the PNS), satellite cells (around ganglion cells).

## 1.12 Basic principles of cell injury and adaptation

When a cell meets stress it first tries to **adapt**. If the stress is too severe or lasts too long, the cell is **injured**; mild injury is **reversible**, but severe injury is **irreversible** and ends in **cell death**.

```text
Normal cell --(increased demand or stimulus)--> ADAPTATION (hypertrophy, hyperplasia,
     |                                           atrophy, metaplasia)
     |--(injurious agent, mild)--> REVERSIBLE INJURY (cell swelling, fatty change)
     |                                 |  stimulus removed -> recovery
     |--(severe or persistent)----> IRREVERSIBLE INJURY --> CELL DEATH
                                                         (necrosis or apoptosis)
```

### Causes of cellular injury

1. **Oxygen deprivation:** hypoxia (low oxygen, as in anaemia, lung disease, carbon monoxide poisoning) and ischaemia (reduced blood supply; the most common cause, as in myocardial infarction).
2. **Physical agents:** trauma, extremes of temperature (burns, frostbite), radiation, electric shock, sudden pressure change.
3. **Chemical agents and drugs:** poisons, alcohol, overdose of drugs such as paracetamol, environmental pollutants, even excess salt or glucose.
4. **Infectious agents:** viruses, bacteria and their toxins, fungi, parasites.
5. **Immunological reactions:** autoimmune disease, allergy (anaphylaxis).
6. **Genetic defects:** sickle cell disease, inborn errors of metabolism.
7. **Nutritional imbalance:** protein-energy malnutrition, vitamin deficiencies; also excess (obesity, atherosclerosis).
8. **Ageing.**

### Pathogenesis: mechanisms of cell injury

| Target | What goes wrong | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Cell membrane damage** | Free radicals cause lipid peroxidation; phospholipases activated by calcium break down membrane lipids; toxins and complement punch holes | Loss of selective permeability, entry of Ca²⁺ and water, leakage of enzymes, damaged lysosomal membranes release enzymes that digest the cell |
| **Mitochondrial damage** | Hypoxia, toxins and Ca²⁺ overload open the mitochondrial permeability transition pore | Fall in ATP; Na⁺/K⁺ pump fails (Na⁺ and water enter → swelling); anaerobic glycolysis → lactic acid and fall in pH; release of cytochrome c starts apoptosis |
| **Ribosome damage** | Lack of ATP makes ribosomes detach from rough ER; some toxins act on ribosomes | Reduced protein synthesis; lipid accumulates (fatty change) because apoproteins are not made |
| **Nuclear damage** | Radiation, free radicals, drugs damage DNA | Failed repair triggers apoptosis; nuclear changes of necrosis (pyknosis, karyorrhexis, karyolysis) |

Common pathways: ATP depletion, influx of calcium (activates damaging enzymes), free radical (reactive oxygen species) formation, and defects in membrane permeability.

### Morphology of cell injury: adaptive changes

| Adaptation | Definition | Physiological example | Pathological example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Atrophy** | Decrease in cell size and function | Shrinking of uterus after delivery, thymus in adults | Disuse atrophy of a limb in plaster, loss of nerve supply, reduced blood supply, starvation |
| **Hypertrophy** | Increase in cell size, so organ size increases (no new cells) | Skeletal muscle of athletes, uterus in pregnancy | Left ventricle in hypertension or aortic stenosis |
| **Hyperplasia** | Increase in cell number (only in cells that can divide) | Breast at puberty and lactation, liver regeneration | Endometrial hyperplasia from excess oestrogen, benign prostatic hyperplasia, skin warts |
| **Metaplasia** | Replacement of one adult cell type by another better able to stand stress | — | Ciliated columnar epithelium of bronchi changing to squamous epithelium in smokers; squamous epithelium of lower oesophagus changing to columnar in acid reflux (Barrett's oesophagus) |
| **Dysplasia** | Disordered growth: variation in cell size and shape, large dark nuclei, loss of normal arrangement | — | Cervix, bronchi in smokers; can progress to cancer, so it is called a pre-cancerous change |

Hypertrophy and hyperplasia often occur together (uterus in pregnancy). Metaplasia and early dysplasia can reverse if the stimulus is removed.

### Cell swelling

The first and commonest sign of reversible injury (also called hydropic change or vacuolar degeneration). Cause: ATP falls, the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump fails, Na⁺ and water enter the cell. The cell looks pale and enlarged; the organ becomes heavier and paler. It is fully reversible if the cause is removed.

### Intracellular accumulations

Abnormal amounts of substances collect inside cells when they are produced too fast, removed too slowly or cannot be broken down.

| Substance | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Lipids (fatty change, steatosis) | Fatty liver in alcoholism, malnutrition, diabetes, obesity |
| Cholesterol | Foam cells in atherosclerotic plaques; xanthomas in skin |
| Proteins | Protein droplets in kidney tubules in heavy proteinuria |
| Glycogen | Diabetes, glycogen storage diseases |
| Pigments – exogenous | Carbon (anthracosis in lungs of city dwellers and miners), tattoo ink |
| Pigments – endogenous | Lipofuscin ("wear-and-tear" pigment of ageing), melanin, haemosiderin (iron overload), bilirubin (jaundice) |

**Pathological calcification:** dystrophic (in dead or damaged tissue with normal blood calcium, e.g. atheroma, damaged heart valves) and metastatic (in normal tissue when blood calcium is high, e.g. hyperparathyroidism).

### Cell death

| Feature | Necrosis | Apoptosis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nature | Always pathological, accidental | Programmed; physiological or pathological |
| Cells involved | Groups of cells | Single cells |
| Cell size | Swelling | Shrinkage |
| Membrane | Breaks, contents leak | Stays intact; apoptotic bodies formed |
| Nucleus | Pyknosis (shrinks), karyorrhexis (breaks up), karyolysis (fades) | Chromatin condenses and fragments |
| Inflammation | Present | Absent (bodies eaten by macrophages) |
| Examples | Myocardial infarction, gangrene | Shedding of endometrium, removal of self-reactive lymphocytes, cell turnover |

**Types of necrosis:** coagulative (most organs after ischaemia, e.g. heart, kidney; outline preserved), liquefactive (brain infarcts, abscesses), caseous (tuberculosis, cheese-like), fat necrosis (acute pancreatitis), fibrinoid (vessel walls in severe hypertension), and gangrene (necrosis with putrefaction: dry, wet or gas gangrene).

Damaged cells leak enzymes into blood; measuring them helps diagnosis, for example troponins and creatine kinase-MB after heart muscle injury, and liver transaminases (ALT, AST) after liver injury.

## 1.13 Common medical terminology

| Term | Meaning | Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| -itis | Inflammation (arthritis, dermatitis) | -algia | Pain (neuralgia) |
| -emia / -aemia | Condition of blood (anaemia, hyperglycaemia) | -osis | Abnormal condition (osteoporosis, thrombosis) |
| -ectomy | Surgical removal (appendicectomy) | -otomy | Cutting into (tracheotomy) |
| -plasia | Formation, growth (hyperplasia) | -trophy | Nourishment, growth (atrophy) |
| -penia | Deficiency (leucopenia, thrombocytopenia) | -cyte | Cell (erythrocyte) |
| -megaly | Enlargement (splenomegaly, cardiomegaly) | -oma | Tumour (lipoma, carcinoma) |
| Brady- / tachy- | Slow / fast (bradycardia, tachycardia) | Hyper- / hypo- | Above / below normal |
| Dys- | Difficult, abnormal (dyspnoea, dysplasia) | Hemi- | Half (hemiplegia) |
| Acute | Sudden onset, short course | Chronic | Slow onset, long course |
| Syndrome | Set of signs and symptoms occurring together | Idiopathic | Of unknown cause |
| Iatrogenic | Caused by medical treatment | Prognosis | Expected outcome |

## Remember

- Anatomy = structure, physiology = function, pathophysiology = disordered function in disease.
- Six levels of organisation: chemical → cellular → tissue → organ → system → organism.
- Negative feedback restores (blood pressure, glucose, temperature); positive feedback amplifies (labour, clotting).
- Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase moves 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in using ATP; 0.9% NaCl is isotonic with blood.
- Four signalling forms: contact-dependent, paracrine, synaptic, endocrine.
- Four tissues: epithelial, connective, muscular, nervous.
- Adaptations: atrophy (smaller), hypertrophy (bigger cells), hyperplasia (more cells), metaplasia (cell type change), dysplasia (disordered, pre-cancerous).
- Mechanisms of injury hit membranes, mitochondria (ATP falls), ribosomes (protein synthesis falls) and the nucleus.
- Cell swelling is the earliest reversible change; necrosis is messy and inflammatory, apoptosis is tidy and silent.
