# Unit 2: Skin and wound healing, skeletal system, muscle, joints and their diseases

This unit covers the body's outer covering and its frame. It starts with the skin, three skin diseases (psoriasis, dermatitis and leprosy) and how wounds heal. It then describes the skeleton, skeletal muscle and how it contracts, the neuromuscular junction, and joints. It ends with three common bone and joint diseases: rheumatoid arthritis, osteoporosis and gout.

## 2.1 Structure of the skin

The skin (integument) is the largest organ of the body, about 1.5–2 m² in an adult. It has two layers, the **epidermis** and the **dermis**, resting on the **hypodermis** (subcutaneous tissue), which is not part of the skin proper.

```text
 Surface  ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
          | stratum corneum   (dead keratin-filled cells)  |
 EPIDERMIS| stratum lucidum   (thick skin only)            |
          | stratum granulosum (keratohyalin granules)     |
          | stratum spinosum  (desmosomes, Langerhans cells)|
          | stratum basale    (dividing cells, melanocytes) |
          |----------------- basement membrane ------------|
 DERMIS   | papillary layer  (loose tissue, capillary loops, Meissner corpuscles)
          | reticular layer  (dense collagen, hair follicles, sweat and sebaceous
          |                   glands, blood vessels, nerves, Pacinian corpuscles)
 HYPODERMIS  adipose and areolar tissue, larger vessels
```

### Epidermis

Keratinised stratified squamous epithelium with no blood vessels. Its cells are:

| Cell | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Keratinocytes (about 90%) | Make keratin, a tough waterproof protein; move up and die as they mature |
| Melanocytes (stratum basale) | Make melanin, which protects DNA from ultraviolet light |
| Langerhans cells | Pick up antigens and take part in immune responses |
| Merkel cells | Touch receptors |

New cells are made in the stratum basale and take about four weeks to reach the surface and flake off.

### Dermis

Dense irregular connective tissue with collagen and elastic fibres, giving strength and stretch. It contains blood vessels, lymphatics, nerves, sensory receptors, hair follicles with arrector pili muscles, sebaceous glands (secrete sebum into hair follicles) and sweat glands (eccrine all over the body for temperature control; apocrine in axilla and groin, opening into hair follicles).

## 2.2 Functions of the skin

1. **Protection** – against mechanical injury, microbes (acid mantle, keratin), chemicals, ultraviolet light (melanin) and water loss.
2. **Temperature regulation** – sweating, and widening or narrowing of skin blood vessels.
3. **Sensation** – touch, pressure, pain, heat and cold receptors.
4. **Excretion** – small amounts of water, salts and urea in sweat.
5. **Synthesis of vitamin D** – ultraviolet light converts 7-dehydrocholesterol in skin to cholecalciferol.
6. **Immunity** – Langerhans cells.
7. **Absorption** – lipid-soluble substances; the basis of ointments and transdermal patches.
8. **Blood reservoir** – the dermal vessels hold a good fraction of blood volume.

## 2.3 Skin disorders

### Psoriasis

**Definition:** a chronic, relapsing, immune-mediated inflammatory skin disease with well-defined red plaques covered by silvery scales.

**Aetiology:**
- Genetic tendency (runs in families; linked with HLA-Cw6).
- Triggers: streptococcal throat infection, skin injury (new lesions at the site of trauma, the Koebner phenomenon), stress, cold dry weather, alcohol, smoking, and some drugs (lithium, beta blockers, antimalarials, withdrawal of systemic corticosteroids).

**Pathogenesis:**

```text
Genetic tendency + trigger
      -> dendritic cells in skin activated
      -> release IL-12 and IL-23 -> activate Th1 and Th17 lymphocytes
      -> cytokines: TNF-alpha, IL-17, IL-22, interferon-gamma
      -> keratinocytes divide very fast (epidermal turnover falls from about
         4 weeks to a few days) and do not mature properly
      -> thick epidermis, nuclei kept in surface layer (parakeratosis),
         dilated dermal capillaries, neutrophils in epidermis
      -> red, raised, scaly plaques
```

**Clinical features:** sharply demarcated red plaques with silvery white scales on extensor surfaces (elbows, knees), scalp and lower back; scraping the scale shows pinpoint bleeding (Auspitz sign); nail pitting and separation; itching may be present. About a fifth to a third of patients develop psoriatic arthritis. Types: plaque (commonest), guttate (small drop-like lesions after throat infection), pustular, erythrodermic, inverse (skin folds).

### Dermatitis (eczema)

**Definition:** inflammation of the skin with itching, redness, oedema, vesicles and oozing in the acute stage, and thickened, dry, scaly skin (lichenification) in the chronic stage.

| Type | Cause and mechanism |
| --- | --- |
| **Atopic dermatitis** | Inherited tendency to allergy (with asthma and hay fever); defective skin barrier (filaggrin defect), Th2 response with IgE; childhood onset; flexures of elbows and knees |
| **Irritant contact dermatitis** | Direct damage by detergents, soaps, solvents, acids, alkalis; no immune memory needed; common in hands of cleaners and health workers |
| **Allergic contact dermatitis** | Type IV (delayed, T-cell mediated) hypersensitivity to nickel, chromium (cement), rubber, hair dyes, topical medicines; appears 24–72 hours after contact in a sensitised person |
| **Seborrhoeic dermatitis** | Greasy scales on scalp (dandruff), face, chest; linked to Malassezia yeast |
| **Photodermatitis** | Sun exposure with a drug or chemical |

**Pathogenesis (common pattern):** the irritant or allergen damages keratinocytes or activates immune cells → release of inflammatory mediators → dilated vessels, oedema between epidermal cells (spongiosis) → vesicles, oozing, itching; scratching thickens the skin.

### Pathophysiology of leprosy

**Definition:** a chronic infectious disease caused by *Mycobacterium leprae*, affecting mainly skin and peripheral nerves.

**Aetiology:** *M. leprae*, an acid-fast bacillus that grows very slowly (generation time about 12–14 days) and prefers cooler parts of the body; it cannot be grown on artificial media. Spread is mainly by droplets from the nose of untreated patients after prolonged close contact. The incubation period is long, usually years. Most exposed people do not develop disease because of good immunity.

**Pathogenesis:** the bacilli enter Schwann cells of peripheral nerves and macrophages in the skin. The type of disease depends on the patient's cell-mediated immunity.

| Feature | Tuberculoid leprosy | Lepromatous leprosy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cell-mediated immunity | Strong (Th1) | Weak (Th2) |
| Bacilli | Few (paucibacillary) | Many (multibacillary) |
| Skin lesions | One or a few well-defined, pale or red, dry, hairless anaesthetic patches | Many symmetrical nodules and plaques; thickened facial skin (leonine face), loss of eyebrows |
| Nerves | Early, marked damage near lesions; thickened nerves | Slow, symmetrical glove-and-stocking loss |
| Lepromin test | Positive | Negative |
| Infectivity | Low | High |

Borderline forms lie between the two. Nerve damage causes loss of sensation, so painless injuries, burns and ulcers occur; muscle weakness causes claw hand, foot drop and eye problems. Loss of fingers and toes is due to repeated unnoticed injury and infection, not to the bacillus "eating" them. Immune reactions (type 1 reversal reaction and type 2 reaction, erythema nodosum leprosum) can occur. Leprosy is curable with multidrug therapy and is notifiable in India.

## 2.4 Basic principles of wound healing

**Healing** is the replacement of destroyed tissue by living tissue. It happens by **regeneration** (replacement by the same type of cells, possible in tissues whose cells can divide, such as epidermis and liver) or by **repair** (replacement by fibrous connective tissue, forming a scar).

### Phases of wound healing

| Phase | Time | Main events |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Haemostasis | Minutes | Vessel constriction, platelet plug, fibrin clot seals the wound |
| Inflammation | Day 1–3 | Neutrophils, then macrophages, clean debris and bacteria; macrophages release growth factors |
| Proliferation | Day 3 to about 3 weeks | Granulation tissue (new capillaries plus fibroblasts) fills the gap; fibroblasts lay down collagen; epithelial cells cover the surface; myofibroblasts pull the edges together (contraction) |
| Maturation (remodelling) | Weeks to a year or more | Collagen reorganised and cross-linked; scar becomes paler and stronger, reaching about 70–80% of original strength |

### Healing by first and second intention

| Feature | First (primary) intention | Second (secondary) intention |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wound | Clean, edges close together (surgical incision with sutures) | Large, gaping, infected, tissue lost (ulcers, burns) |
| Granulation tissue | Little | Abundant, fills from the base |
| Contraction | Minimal | Marked |
| Scar | Thin, neat | Large, may deform |
| Time | Short | Long |

**Factors affecting wound healing.** Local: infection (most important), poor blood supply, foreign bodies, movement, large gap, radiation. Systemic: age, poor nutrition (protein, vitamin C, zinc), diabetes, corticosteroid treatment, anaemia, poor circulation, immune deficiency.

**Complications:** wound infection, keloid (excess scar beyond the wound margin), contractures, wound breakdown (dehiscence), incisional hernia.

## 2.5 Skeletal system: divisions and functions

The adult skeleton has 206 bones.

**Functions:** support, protection of organs (skull, rib cage), movement (bones act as levers for muscles), mineral store (calcium and phosphate), blood cell formation (red bone marrow), and fat storage (yellow marrow).

| Division | Number | Bones |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Axial skeleton** | 80 | Skull (cranium 8, face 14), 6 ear ossicles, hyoid (1), vertebral column (26 in adult), thoracic cage (sternum 1, ribs 24) |
| **Appendicular skeleton** | 126 | Pectoral girdles (clavicle and scapula, 4), upper limbs (60), pelvic girdle (hip bones, 2), lower limbs (60) |

## 2.6 Types of bones

| Type | Shape | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Long | Longer than wide; shaft (diaphysis) and two ends (epiphyses) | Femur, humerus, radius, phalanges |
| Short | Cube-like | Carpals, tarsals |
| Flat | Thin, flat, often curved | Skull vault bones, sternum, ribs, scapula |
| Irregular | Complex shapes | Vertebrae, some facial bones |
| Sesamoid | Develop inside tendons | Patella |
| Sutural (Wormian) | Small bones in skull sutures | Variable |

**Parts of a long bone:** diaphysis (shaft of compact bone around the medullary cavity with yellow marrow), epiphyses (spongy bone with red marrow, covered by articular cartilage), metaphysis with the epiphyseal (growth) plate in children, periosteum (outer membrane for growth in width, repair and attachment) and endosteum (lines the cavity).

**Bone tissue:** compact bone is made of osteons (Haversian systems: concentric lamellae around a central canal with vessels); spongy bone is a network of trabeculae with red marrow between them. Bone cells: osteoprogenitor cells, osteoblasts (build bone), osteocytes (mature cells in lacunae), osteoclasts (large multinucleated cells that resorb bone). Bone is constantly remodelled by osteoblasts and osteoclasts under the control of parathyroid hormone, calcitonin, vitamin D, oestrogen and mechanical stress.

## 2.7 Salient features of the axial skeleton

**Skull.** Cranial bones: frontal, two parietal, two temporal, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid. They are joined by immovable joints called sutures (coronal, sagittal, lambdoid). The occipital bone has the foramen magnum through which the spinal cord passes. The temporal bone houses the middle and inner ear. Facial bones: two nasal, two maxillae, two zygomatic, mandible (the only movable skull bone), two lacrimal, two palatine, two inferior nasal conchae, vomer. In the newborn, gaps called fontanelles allow the skull to mould during birth.

**Vertebral column.** 33 vertebrae in a child (7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 fused sacral, about 4 fused coccygeal), counted as 26 in the adult. A typical vertebra has a body, a vertebral arch (pedicles and laminae) enclosing the vertebral foramen, a spinous process, two transverse processes and articular processes. Special features: cervical vertebrae have foramina in their transverse processes; the atlas (C1) has no body and holds the skull; the axis (C2) has the dens on which the atlas turns; thoracic vertebrae have facets for ribs; lumbar vertebrae have large bodies to bear weight. The column has four curves (cervical and lumbar forward, thoracic and sacral backward) and intervertebral discs of fibrocartilage.

**Thoracic cage.** Sternum (manubrium, body, xiphoid process) and 12 pairs of ribs: true ribs 1–7 joined directly to the sternum by costal cartilage, false ribs 8–10 joined indirectly, floating ribs 11–12 not joined in front. Protects heart and lungs and helps breathing.

## 2.8 Salient features of the appendicular skeleton

| Region | Bones and key features |
| --- | --- |
| Pectoral girdle | Clavicle (S-shaped strut, commonly fractured); scapula (flat triangular bone with spine, acromion, coracoid process and glenoid cavity for the humerus) |
| Arm | Humerus: head fits the glenoid cavity; surgical neck; deltoid tuberosity; trochlea and capitulum at the elbow |
| Forearm | Radius (lateral, thumb side) and ulna (medial; olecranon process forms the elbow point) |
| Hand | 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals, 14 phalanges |
| Pelvic girdle | Two hip bones, each formed by fusion of ilium, ischium and pubis; acetabulum for the head of femur; joined in front at the pubic symphysis and behind to the sacrum. The female pelvis is wider with a rounder inlet, suited to childbirth |
| Thigh | Femur, the longest and strongest bone: head, neck (common fracture site in the elderly), greater and lesser trochanters, two condyles at the knee |
| Knee | Patella (sesamoid bone in the quadriceps tendon) |
| Leg | Tibia (medial, weight-bearing, medial malleolus) and fibula (lateral, lateral malleolus) |
| Foot | 7 tarsals (talus, calcaneus or heel bone, and others), 5 metatarsals, 14 phalanges; arches spread body weight |

## 2.9 Organisation of skeletal muscle

```text
Muscle (covered by epimysium)
  -> fascicles (bundles, covered by perimysium)
     -> muscle fibres (cells, covered by endomysium; many nuclei)
        -> myofibrils (rows of sarcomeres)
           -> myofilaments: thick (myosin) and thin (actin, tropomyosin, troponin)
```

Each fibre has a cell membrane called the **sarcolemma**, which dips inward as **transverse (T) tubules**, and a **sarcoplasmic reticulum** that stores calcium. A T tubule with the two terminal cisternae of sarcoplasmic reticulum on either side is a **triad**.

**Sarcomere** (the unit of contraction, between two Z lines):

```text
 Z|-------- I band --------|=========== A band ===========|-------- I band -----|Z
  |  thin (actin) only     |  thick (myosin) + overlap     |                     |
  |                        |      | H zone | M line        |                     |
```

During contraction the I band and H zone shorten, the A band stays the same length, and the Z lines come closer.

## 2.10 Physiology of muscle contraction (sliding filament theory)

1. A nerve impulse reaches the neuromuscular junction and acetylcholine is released.
2. An action potential spreads along the sarcolemma and down the T tubules.
3. The sarcoplasmic reticulum releases Ca²⁺ into the cytoplasm.
4. Ca²⁺ binds troponin C; tropomyosin moves off the myosin-binding sites on actin.
5. Myosin heads (already energised by splitting ATP) bind actin, forming **cross-bridges**.
6. **Power stroke:** the heads pivot and pull the thin filaments towards the centre of the sarcomere; ADP and phosphate are released.
7. A new ATP binds and the myosin head detaches; ATP is split and the head is re-cocked. The cycle repeats while Ca²⁺ and ATP are present.
8. **Relaxation:** acetylcholinesterase destroys acetylcholine; Ca²⁺ is pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum (Ca²⁺-ATPase); tropomyosin again covers the binding sites.

Without ATP the heads cannot detach, which explains the stiffness of rigor mortis after death.

**Energy sources:** creatine phosphate (seconds), anaerobic glycolysis (producing lactic acid), aerobic respiration in mitochondria (long-lasting). **Types of contraction:** isotonic (muscle shortens, tension constant) and isometric (tension rises, length constant). Other terms: twitch, summation, tetanus (sustained contraction), muscle tone, fatigue, motor unit (one motor neuron and the fibres it supplies).

## 2.11 Neuromuscular junction

The junction between a motor neuron and a skeletal muscle fibre.

```text
 motor axon terminal (synaptic vesicles with ACh)
   ||  ACh released by exocytosis when Ca2+ enters
   vv
 ---------- synaptic cleft (acetylcholinesterase here) ----------
 motor end plate (folded sarcolemma with nicotinic ACh receptors)
   -> Na+ enters -> end-plate potential -> muscle action potential
```

Steps: the impulse opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels in the terminal → Ca²⁺ entry causes vesicles to release acetylcholine → acetylcholine binds nicotinic (Nm) receptors on the motor end plate → Na⁺ enters, producing an end-plate potential → a muscle action potential starts → acetylcholinesterase rapidly breaks acetylcholine into choline and acetate, ending the signal.

**Clinical links:** myasthenia gravis (autoantibodies destroy acetylcholine receptors → fatiguable weakness, drooping eyelids); neuromuscular blocking drugs used in surgery act here; anticholinesterases prolong acetylcholine action; botulinum toxin blocks acetylcholine release.

## 2.12 Joints: structural and functional classification

**Functional classification:**

| Type | Movement | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Synarthrosis | Immovable | Skull sutures |
| Amphiarthrosis | Slightly movable | Intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis |
| Diarthrosis | Freely movable | Knee, shoulder (all synovial joints) |

**Structural classification:**

| Type | Bones joined by | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fibrous | Dense fibrous tissue | Sutures; syndesmosis (distal tibiofibular joint); gomphosis (tooth in socket) |
| Cartilaginous | Cartilage | Synchondrosis (epiphyseal plate, first rib–sternum); symphysis (pubic symphysis, intervertebral discs) |
| Synovial | Joint cavity with synovial fluid | Knee, hip, elbow |

**Synovial joint structure:** articular (hyaline) cartilage on bone ends, a joint cavity, an articular capsule (outer fibrous layer and inner synovial membrane that secretes synovial fluid for lubrication and nourishment), ligaments, and in some joints menisci and bursae.

**Types of synovial joints:**

| Type | Movement | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plane (gliding) | Sliding | Intercarpal joints |
| Hinge | Flexion and extension in one plane | Elbow, knee, interphalangeal |
| Pivot | Rotation around one axis | Atlas on axis, proximal radioulnar |
| Condyloid (ellipsoid) | Two planes | Wrist (radiocarpal) |
| Saddle | Two planes, wide range | Carpometacarpal joint of thumb |
| Ball and socket | All directions, including rotation | Shoulder, hip |

## 2.13 Diseases of bones and joints

### Rheumatoid arthritis

**Definition:** a chronic systemic autoimmune disease causing symmetrical inflammation of synovial joints, mainly small joints of hands and feet, leading to joint destruction.

**Aetiology:** genetic tendency (HLA-DR4 and related genes), female sex (about three times commoner in women), smoking, and possibly infections that trigger autoimmunity. Autoantibodies: rheumatoid factor (IgM against the Fc part of IgG) and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies.

**Pathogenesis:**

```text
Genetic tendency + trigger (e.g. smoking -> citrullinated proteins)
  -> loss of tolerance: T cells and B cells react to joint antigens
  -> CD4 T cells activate macrophages and B cells; autoantibodies and immune complexes
  -> cytokines TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6 -> synovial inflammation
  -> synovium thickens into a pannus (inflamed granulation tissue)
  -> pannus erodes cartilage and bone; osteoclasts activated
  -> joint destruction, deformity, fibrous or bony fusion (ankylosis)
```

**Clinical features:** symmetrical pain and swelling of small joints (proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal, wrists), morning stiffness lasting more than an hour, fatigue, low-grade fever. Deformities: ulnar deviation, swan-neck and boutonnière deformity. Extra-articular: rheumatoid nodules, anaemia, lung fibrosis, vasculitis, dry eyes. Raised ESR and CRP.

### Osteoporosis

**Definition:** a systemic skeletal disease with low bone mass and deterioration of bone microarchitecture, causing fragile bones and a high risk of fracture. The bone that is present is normally mineralised, but there is too little of it.

**Aetiology:**
- **Primary:** postmenopausal (loss of oestrogen) and senile (ageing).
- **Secondary:** long-term corticosteroid therapy, hyperthyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, immobilisation, low calcium and vitamin D intake, smoking, alcohol, low body weight, some drugs (heparin, some anticonvulsants).

**Pathogenesis:** peak bone mass is reached in early adulthood; afterwards resorption by osteoclasts slowly exceeds formation by osteoblasts. Oestrogen normally restrains osteoclasts (it reduces RANKL and raises osteoprotegerin); after menopause its loss increases cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF) and RANKL, so osteoclast activity and bone loss rise quickly, especially in spongy bone. Ageing reduces osteoblast activity and calcium absorption. Thin, broken trabeculae make the bone weak.

**Clinical features:** often silent until a fracture. Typical fractures: vertebral compression (loss of height, kyphosis or "dowager's hump", back pain), neck of femur after minor falls, distal radius (Colles' fracture). Diagnosis by bone mineral density (DEXA scan; T-score of −2.5 or lower).

### Gout

**Definition:** a disorder of purine metabolism in which high uric acid in blood (hyperuricaemia) leads to deposition of monosodium urate crystals in joints and tissues, causing attacks of acute arthritis.

**Aetiology:**
- **Overproduction of uric acid:** high purine diet (red meat, organ meats, seafood), alcohol (especially beer), rapid cell breakdown (cancer chemotherapy, leukaemia), enzyme defects.
- **Under-excretion (commoner):** kidney disease, diuretics (thiazides), low-dose aspirin, dehydration, lead.
- More common in men; obesity and metabolic syndrome increase the risk.

**Pathogenesis:**

```text
Purines -> hypoxanthine -> xanthine -> uric acid (enzyme xanthine oxidase)
High blood urate -> supersaturation -> urate crystals form in cooler,
  less vascular joints (big toe)
  -> crystals engulfed by neutrophils and macrophages
  -> NLRP3 inflammasome activated -> IL-1 beta released
  -> intense acute inflammation (acute gouty arthritis)
Repeated attacks -> chronic arthritis, tophi (urate deposits in ear, joints),
  urate kidney stones and kidney damage
```

**Clinical features:** sudden, very painful, red, hot swollen joint, often the first metatarsophalangeal joint of the big toe (podagra), frequently at night after a heavy meal or alcohol; attacks settle over days; between attacks the patient is free of symptoms. Diagnosis: needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals in joint fluid.

| Feature | Rheumatoid arthritis | Gout | Osteoporosis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Basic problem | Autoimmune synovitis | Urate crystal deposition | Low bone mass |
| Typical site | Small joints, symmetrical | Big toe, one joint | Spine, hip, wrist |
| Sex | More in women | More in men | More in women after menopause |
| Key test | RF, anti-CCP | Joint fluid crystals, serum uric acid | DEXA scan |

## Remember

- Epidermis (5 layers in thick skin) has no vessels; melanocytes and dividing cells sit in the stratum basale.
- Skin makes vitamin D and regulates temperature.
- Psoriasis = fast keratinocyte turnover driven by Th17/IL-23 and TNF; silvery plaques on extensor surfaces.
- Contact allergic dermatitis is type IV hypersensitivity; atopic dermatitis is a barrier defect with Th2 allergy.
- Leprosy: *M. leprae* in Schwann cells; tuberculoid (strong immunity, few bacilli) vs lepromatous (weak immunity, many bacilli).
- Wound healing: haemostasis → inflammation → proliferation (granulation tissue) → remodelling.
- 206 bones: axial 80, appendicular 126.
- Contraction: Ca²⁺ binds troponin, cross-bridges form, ATP is needed to detach myosin.
- NMJ uses acetylcholine on nicotinic receptors; acetylcholinesterase ends the signal.
- RA = pannus; gout = urate crystals and IL-1β; osteoporosis = resorption exceeds formation, oestrogen loss.

# Unit 3: Blood, lymphatic system, inflammation and repair, and haematological diseases

Blood is the transport medium of the body and the tissue most often sampled in the laboratory. This unit covers body fluids, the make-up and functions of blood, how blood cells and haemoglobin are formed, how blood clots, blood groups and transfusion, and the lymphatic system. It then explains inflammation and repair, the body's response to injury, and finally the main blood diseases: the anaemias and haemophilia.

## 3.1 Body fluids

Water makes up about 60% of body weight in an adult man (less in women and the elderly, more in infants).

```text
Total body water (about 60% of body weight, ~42 L in a 70 kg man)
  |-- Intracellular fluid (ICF): about two-thirds (~40% of body weight)
  |-- Extracellular fluid (ECF): about one-third (~20% of body weight)
         |-- Interstitial fluid (tissue fluid, lymph): about three-quarters of ECF
         |-- Plasma: about one-quarter of ECF (~3 L)
         |-- Transcellular fluid: CSF, synovial, pleural, aqueous humour, digestive juices
```

| Ion | ECF | ICF |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Main cation | Na⁺ | K⁺ |
| Main anion | Cl⁻, HCO3⁻ | Phosphates, proteins |

The difference is kept by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pump. Water moves between compartments by osmosis; between plasma and tissue fluid it moves under the balance of capillary hydrostatic pressure (pushes fluid out) and plasma colloid osmotic pressure (pulls fluid in), as described by Starling.

## 3.2 Composition of blood

Blood is a fluid connective tissue. Total volume is about 5–6 L in an adult (about 7–8% of body weight). Normal pH 7.35–7.45; it is denser and more viscous than water.

| Component | Share | Contents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Plasma** | About 55% | Water (about 91%); plasma proteins (about 7%: albumin, globulins, fibrinogen); nutrients, electrolytes, hormones, gases, waste (urea, creatinine) |
| **Formed elements** | About 45% (haematocrit) | Red blood cells, white blood cells, platelets |

**Serum** is plasma without clotting factors (the fluid left after blood clots).

**Plasma proteins:**

| Protein | Made in | Function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Albumin | Liver | Colloid osmotic pressure (keeps fluid in vessels), carries drugs, bilirubin, fatty acids |
| Globulins (α, β, γ) | Liver; γ-globulins by plasma cells | Transport (α and β), antibodies (γ) |
| Fibrinogen | Liver | Clotting (converted to fibrin) |

Low albumin (liver disease, malnutrition, kidney disease with protein loss) causes oedema. Many drugs bind albumin, which affects how much free drug is available.

### Formed elements

| Cell | Normal count | Structure | Life span | Function |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Red cells (erythrocytes) | About 4.5–5.5 million/µL in men, 4–5 million/µL in women | Biconcave discs about 7.5 µm, no nucleus, full of haemoglobin | About 120 days | Carry O2 and some CO2; buffering |
| White cells (leucocytes) | 4,000–11,000/µL | Nucleated | Hours to years | Defence |
| Platelets (thrombocytes) | 1.5–4 lakh/µL | Cell fragments from megakaryocytes | About 7–10 days | Haemostasis |

**White cells:**

| Type | Share | Features | Function |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Neutrophils | 50–70% | Multilobed nucleus, fine granules | First phagocytes in acute infection |
| Eosinophils | 1–4% | Bilobed nucleus, red granules | Parasites, allergy |
| Basophils | 0–1% | Blue granules with histamine and heparin | Allergic reactions |
| Lymphocytes | 20–40% | Large round nucleus | B cells (antibodies), T cells (cell-mediated immunity), NK cells |
| Monocytes | 2–8% | Kidney-shaped nucleus | Become macrophages in tissues |

Normal haemoglobin: about 13–17 g/dL in men and 12–15 g/dL in women.

## 3.3 Functions of blood

1. Transport of oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrients, hormones, waste and drugs.
2. Regulation of pH (buffers such as bicarbonate and haemoglobin), body temperature (carries heat) and water balance.
3. Protection: defence by white cells and antibodies, and prevention of blood loss by clotting.

## 3.4 Haemopoiesis

**Haemopoiesis** is the formation of blood cells. In the embryo it occurs in the yolk sac, then the liver and spleen, and from late fetal life in the bone marrow. In adults it happens in the red marrow of flat bones (sternum, ribs, vertebrae, pelvis, skull) and the ends of long bones (femur, humerus).

```text
                    Pluripotent haemopoietic stem cell
                   /                                  \
       Myeloid stem cell                          Lymphoid stem cell
   /      |        |          \                    /          \
proerythroblast  myeloblast  monoblast  megakaryoblast   B lymphocyte  T lymphocyte
   |              |           |           |                (plasma cells) (thymus)
reticulocyte  neutrophil,   monocyte   megakaryocyte
   |          eosinophil,      |           |
red cell      basophil     macrophage   platelets
```

**Erythropoiesis** (red cell formation): proerythroblast → early, intermediate and late normoblasts (haemoglobin builds up, nucleus shrinks and is pushed out) → reticulocyte (released into blood) → mature red cell in 1–2 days. It takes about a week.

**Control:** erythropoietin, a hormone made mainly by the kidneys when oxygen delivery falls (anaemia, high altitude, lung disease), stimulates red cell production. White cells are controlled by colony-stimulating factors and interleukins; platelets by thrombopoietin (from the liver).

**Needs for normal red cell formation:** protein, iron, vitamin B12 and folic acid (for DNA synthesis), vitamin C (iron absorption), vitamin B6, copper, cobalt, and thyroid and androgen hormones.

## 3.5 Formation of haemoglobin

Haemoglobin (Hb) is made of four **globin** chains, each with one **haem** group carrying one iron (Fe²⁺) atom; one Hb molecule therefore carries four O2 molecules. Adult Hb (HbA) has two α and two β chains (α2β2); fetal Hb (HbF, α2γ2) binds oxygen more tightly; HbA2 (α2δ2) is a minor form.

```text
Haem synthesis (in mitochondria and cytoplasm of developing red cells)
  succinyl CoA + glycine --(ALA synthase, needs vitamin B6)--> delta-aminolevulinic acid
  -> porphobilinogen -> ... -> protoporphyrin IX
  protoporphyrin IX + Fe2+ --(ferrochelatase)--> haem
Globin chains made on ribosomes
  haem + globin chain -> Hb subunit; four subunits -> haemoglobin
```

**Breakdown:** old red cells are destroyed by macrophages in the spleen and liver. Globin → amino acids (reused); iron → stored as ferritin or carried by transferrin back to the marrow; haem → biliverdin → bilirubin → carried by albumin to the liver → conjugated → excreted in bile. Excess bilirubin causes jaundice.

## 3.6 Mechanisms of coagulation

**Haemostasis** is the stopping of bleeding. Steps:

1. **Vascular spasm** – the injured vessel constricts.
2. **Platelet plug formation** – platelets stick to exposed collagen (helped by von Willebrand factor), change shape, release ADP, thromboxane A2 and serotonin, and attract more platelets (aggregation).
3. **Coagulation** – a cascade of clotting factors converts fibrinogen into fibrin threads, which bind the plug into a firm clot.
4. **Clot retraction and dissolution (fibrinolysis).**

### Clotting factors

| Factor | Name | Factor | Name |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I | Fibrinogen | VIII | Antihaemophilic factor |
| II | Prothrombin | IX | Christmas factor |
| III | Tissue factor (thromboplastin) | X | Stuart–Prower factor |
| IV | Calcium | XI | Plasma thromboplastin antecedent |
| V | Labile factor (proaccelerin) | XII | Hageman factor |
| VII | Stable factor (proconvertin) | XIII | Fibrin-stabilising factor |

(There is no factor VI.) Factors II, VII, IX and X need vitamin K for their synthesis in the liver.

### The cascade

```text
INTRINSIC PATHWAY                      EXTRINSIC PATHWAY
(contact with collagen / glass)        (tissue damage)
XII -> XIIa                            Tissue factor (III) + VII -> VIIa
XI  -> XIa                                    |
IX  -> IXa (+ VIIIa, Ca2+, phospholipid)      |
          \                                   /
           ----------> X -> Xa  <-------------
                COMMON PATHWAY
     Xa + Va + Ca2+ + phospholipid (prothrombinase)
     Prothrombin (II) --------------> Thrombin (IIa)
     Fibrinogen (I) --(thrombin)----> Fibrin monomers
     Fibrin --(XIIIa)--> stable cross-linked fibrin clot
```

Thrombin also activates factors V, VIII, XI and XIII and platelets (positive feedback). The extrinsic pathway is fast (seconds) and is tested by **prothrombin time (PT)**; the intrinsic pathway is slower and tested by **activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT)**.

**Natural anticoagulants:** antithrombin III (inactivates thrombin and Xa; action increased by heparin), protein C and protein S (inactivate Va and VIIIa), prostacyclin from endothelium.

**Fibrinolysis:** plasminogen → plasmin (by tissue plasminogen activator), which digests fibrin into fibrin degradation products.

**Normal values:** bleeding time about 1–6 minutes (platelet function), clotting time about 4–10 minutes (depends on method).

## 3.7 Blood grouping

### ABO system

Red cells carry antigens (agglutinogens) A and/or B; plasma contains naturally occurring antibodies (agglutinins) against the antigen that is absent.

| Group | Antigen on red cells | Antibody in plasma | Can receive red cells from |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | A | Anti-B | A, O |
| B | B | Anti-A | B, O |
| AB | A and B | None | A, B, AB, O (universal recipient) |
| O | None | Anti-A and anti-B | O only (universal donor) |

### Rh factor

The Rh (D) antigen is present on the red cells of about 95% of Indians (Rh-positive). Rh-negative people do not have natural anti-D antibodies; they form them only after exposure to Rh-positive blood (transfusion or pregnancy).

**Haemolytic disease of the newborn (erythroblastosis fetalis):** an Rh-negative mother carrying an Rh-positive fetus is exposed to fetal cells at delivery and forms anti-D. In a later Rh-positive pregnancy, these IgG antibodies cross the placenta and destroy fetal red cells, causing anaemia, jaundice and, in severe cases, hydrops fetalis. It is prevented by giving anti-D immunoglobulin to the mother after delivery of an Rh-positive baby (and after miscarriage or other sensitising events).

## 3.8 Blood transfusion

**Indications:** acute blood loss, severe anaemia, surgery, burns (plasma), bleeding disorders (platelets, clotting factors). Today blood components are usually given instead of whole blood: packed red cells, platelets, fresh frozen plasma, cryoprecipitate.

**Before transfusion:** ABO and Rh grouping of donor and recipient, cross-matching (donor cells with recipient serum), screening of donor blood for HIV, hepatitis B and C, syphilis and malaria.

**Transfusion reactions:**
- Acute haemolytic reaction from ABO mismatch: recipient antibodies destroy donor cells → fever, chills, back pain, low blood pressure, haemoglobin in urine, acute kidney failure, clotting disorders. It can be fatal.
- Febrile and allergic reactions, circulatory overload, transmission of infection, iron overload after many transfusions.

## 3.9 Lymphatic system

### Lymphatic vessels and lymph formation

About 20 L of fluid filters out of blood capillaries each day; about 17 L is reabsorbed, and the remaining 3 L (with proteins that leaked out) enters blind-ended **lymphatic capillaries**. These have overlapping endothelial cells that act as one-way valves. Fluid inside them is called **lymph**: clear, like plasma but with less protein; lymph from the intestine is milky (chyle) because of absorbed fat carried by **lacteals**.

### Circulation of lymph

```text
Lymph capillaries -> lymphatic vessels (with valves) -> lymph nodes
 -> lymph trunks -> two ducts:
    Thoracic duct (from both legs, abdomen, left side of thorax, left arm,
                   left head and neck) -> left subclavian vein
    Right lymphatic duct (right arm, right side of head, neck, thorax)
                   -> right subclavian vein
```

Lymph is moved by the skeletal muscle pump, breathing movements (respiratory pump), contraction of smooth muscle in vessel walls and the valves that prevent backflow.

### Lymphatic organs and tissues

| Organ | Features | Function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Red bone marrow | Primary organ | Forms all blood cells; B cells mature here |
| Thymus | Primary organ above the heart; large in children, shrinks in adults | T cells mature here |
| Lymph nodes | Bean-shaped, along vessels (neck, axilla, groin); cortex with follicles (B cells), paracortex (T cells), medulla | Filter lymph, trap microbes, start immune responses |
| Spleen | Largest lymphatic organ, left upper abdomen; white pulp (lymphocytes) and red pulp (sinusoids) | Filters blood, removes old red cells, immune responses, stores platelets |
| Tonsils, Peyer's patches, appendix (MALT) | Lymphoid tissue under mucous membranes | Defence at body entry points |

### Functions of the lymphatic system

1. Returns excess tissue fluid and leaked proteins to the blood (prevents oedema).
2. Absorbs and transports dietary fats (lacteals).
3. Defence: filters microbes and produces immune responses.

Blocked lymphatics cause **lymphoedema**, for example in filariasis (elephantiasis) or after removal of lymph nodes.

## 3.10 Inflammation: introduction and classification

**Inflammation** is the protective response of living vascularised tissue to injury. It aims to remove the cause (microbes, toxins) and the dead tissue, and to start repair. It can also cause harm (allergy, autoimmune disease).

**Cardinal signs:** rubor (redness), tumor (swelling), calor (heat), dolor (pain) (described by Celsus) and functio laesa (loss of function, added by Virchow).

| Feature | Acute inflammation | Chronic inflammation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Onset | Fast (minutes to hours) | Slow |
| Duration | Days | Weeks to years |
| Main cells | Neutrophils | Lymphocytes, macrophages, plasma cells |
| Tissue changes | Oedema, exudate | Tissue destruction with fibrosis and new vessels |
| Examples | Acute appendicitis, boil, sore throat | Tuberculosis, rheumatoid arthritis, leprosy |

**Granulomatous inflammation** is a special chronic type with collections of activated macrophages (epithelioid cells) and giant cells, as in tuberculosis and leprosy.

## 3.11 Pathophysiology of acute inflammation

### A. Vascular events

1. Brief vasoconstriction of arterioles (seconds).
2. **Vasodilatation** → more blood flow → redness and heat.
3. **Increased vascular permeability** (endothelial cells contract and gaps open) → protein-rich fluid (exudate) leaks into tissue → swelling.
4. Slowing of blood flow (stasis) as fluid is lost and blood becomes thicker.

**Exudate vs transudate:** exudate (inflammation) is rich in protein and cells, specific gravity above 1.020; transudate (heart failure, low albumin) is poor in protein, specific gravity below 1.012.

### B. Cellular events

```text
Margination  (white cells move to the edge of the vessel as flow slows)
 -> Rolling  (loose binding by selectins on endothelium)
 -> Adhesion (firm binding by integrins to ICAM-1, VCAM-1)
 -> Emigration / diapedesis (white cells squeeze between endothelial cells)
 -> Chemotaxis (movement towards chemical attractants: bacterial products,
               C5a, leukotriene B4, IL-8)
 -> Phagocytosis (recognition helped by opsonins such as IgG and C3b,
                  engulfment, killing by oxygen radicals and lysosomal enzymes)
```

Neutrophils arrive first (6–24 hours); monocytes/macrophages follow (24–48 hours).

### Outcomes

Complete resolution (mild injury, little tissue loss); healing by fibrosis (scar); abscess formation (pus walled off); progression to chronic inflammation.

**Systemic effects:** fever (IL-1, TNF and prostaglandin E2 act on the hypothalamus), raised white cell count (leucocytosis), acute phase proteins (CRP), raised ESR, malaise. In severe infection, sepsis and shock.

## 3.12 Mediators of inflammation

| Mediator | Source | Main actions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Histamine** | Mast cells, basophils, platelets | Vasodilatation, increased permeability (immediate), itching |
| **Serotonin (5-HT)** | Platelets | Increased permeability |
| **Prostaglandins** (PGE2, PGI2) | Arachidonic acid via cyclooxygenase (COX) | Vasodilatation, pain, fever |
| **Thromboxane A2** | Platelets (COX pathway) | Platelet aggregation, vasoconstriction |
| **Leukotrienes** (LTB4, LTC4, LTD4, LTE4) | Arachidonic acid via lipoxygenase | LTB4: chemotaxis; LTC4–E4: bronchoconstriction, permeability |
| **Platelet-activating factor** | Many cells | Platelet aggregation, permeability, bronchoconstriction |
| **Cytokines** (IL-1, TNF-α, IL-6) and **chemokines** (IL-8) | Macrophages, lymphocytes | Endothelial activation, fever, acute phase response, chemotaxis |
| **Nitric oxide** | Endothelium, macrophages | Vasodilatation, killing microbes |
| **Lysosomal enzymes and oxygen radicals** | Neutrophils, macrophages | Kill microbes; can damage tissue |
| **Complement** (C3a, C5a, C3b, MAC) | Plasma | C3a/C5a release histamine; C5a chemotaxis; C3b opsonin; membrane attack complex lyses cells |
| **Kinins** (bradykinin) | Plasma (kallikrein system) | Permeability, vasodilatation, pain |
| **Clotting and fibrinolytic products** | Plasma | Fibrinopeptides increase permeability; thrombin activates endothelium |

```text
Membrane phospholipids --(phospholipase A2)--> arachidonic acid
   |-- cyclooxygenase (COX-1, COX-2) --> prostaglandins, prostacyclin, thromboxane A2
   |-- 5-lipoxygenase -----------------> leukotrienes
```

Corticosteroids reduce phospholipase A2 activity and NSAIDs block COX, which is why both reduce inflammation.

## 3.13 Repair

Repair restores tissue after inflammation, by regeneration of the original cells where possible and by fibrosis where not. Tissues are grouped by their ability to divide: **labile** cells (always dividing: epidermis, gut lining, bone marrow), **stable** cells (divide when needed: liver, kidney tubules) and **permanent** cells (cannot divide: neurons, heart muscle, which heal only by scar). Repair by connective tissue passes through granulation tissue, collagen deposition and remodelling (the same steps as wound healing in Unit 2).

## 3.14 Haematological diseases

**Anaemia** is a fall in haemoglobin (or red cell mass) below the normal level for age and sex, reducing the oxygen-carrying capacity of blood. Common symptoms of any anaemia: tiredness, weakness, breathlessness on effort, palpitations, pallor, dizziness, fast heart rate; severe anaemia can cause heart failure.

| Classification by red cell size | MCV | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Microcytic hypochromic | Low | Iron deficiency, thalassaemia |
| Normocytic normochromic | Normal | Acute blood loss, haemolytic, chronic disease |
| Macrocytic | High | Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency (megaloblastic) |

### Iron deficiency anaemia

The commonest anaemia in India and the world, especially in women, children and pregnant women.

**Aetiology:**
1. Low intake: vegetarian diet poor in iron, poverty.
2. Increased need: pregnancy, lactation, growth in infancy and adolescence.
3. Reduced absorption: achlorhydria, gastrectomy, coeliac disease, tea with meals.
4. Chronic blood loss (most important in adults): heavy menstruation, hookworm infestation, bleeding peptic ulcer, piles, colon cancer, long-term NSAID use.

**Pathogenesis:** body iron stores (ferritin) are used up first → serum iron and transferrin saturation fall, total iron-binding capacity rises → too little iron for haem → small (microcytic), pale (hypochromic) red cells and low haemoglobin. Iron is also needed by other tissues, so epithelial changes appear.

**Features:** general anaemia symptoms; koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails), angular stomatitis, glossitis, brittle nails and hair, pica (craving for non-food items like clay or ice), dysphagia from oesophageal webs (Plummer–Vinson syndrome). **Blood:** low Hb, low MCV and MCH, low serum ferritin.

### Megaloblastic anaemia (vitamin B12 and folic acid deficiency)

**Basic defect:** vitamin B12 and folic acid are both needed for DNA synthesis (thymidine formation). When either is lacking, DNA synthesis is slowed but RNA and protein synthesis continue, so the nucleus matures more slowly than the cytoplasm (nuclear–cytoplasmic asynchrony). Red cell precursors become large (**megaloblasts**); many die in the marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis), and those released are large oval red cells (**macrocytes**). Neutrophils show more than five nuclear lobes (hypersegmented). All dividing cells are affected (tongue, gut lining).

| Feature | Vitamin B12 deficiency | Folic acid deficiency |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Causes | Pernicious anaemia (autoimmune loss of intrinsic factor from gastric parietal cells), gastrectomy, ileal disease or resection, strict vegetarian diet, fish tapeworm, long-term metformin or acid suppressants | Poor diet, alcoholism, pregnancy, malabsorption, haemolytic anaemia (high demand), drugs (methotrexate, phenytoin, trimethoprim) |
| Body stores | Large; last several years | Small; last a few months |
| Nervous system | Damaged: subacute combined degeneration of spinal cord, numbness, tingling, loss of position sense, memory loss, depression | Not affected (but low folate in pregnancy causes neural tube defects) |

Vitamin B12 absorption needs intrinsic factor (from the stomach) and the terminal ileum. B12 is also needed to turn methylmalonyl CoA into succinyl CoA; its lack damages myelin. **Features:** anaemia symptoms, mild jaundice (from destroyed precursors), smooth red sore tongue, and in B12 deficiency the neurological signs. Giving folic acid alone in B12 deficiency can improve the blood picture while nerve damage worsens, so the cause must be identified.

### Sickle cell anaemia

**Aetiology:** an inherited (autosomal recessive) disorder in which a single point mutation in the β-globin gene replaces glutamic acid by valine at position 6, producing haemoglobin S (HbS). Homozygotes (HbSS) have the disease; heterozygotes (sickle cell trait, HbAS) are usually healthy and partly protected against falciparum malaria. In India it is common in tribal populations of central, western and southern states.

**Pathogenesis:**

```text
HbS deoxygenated -> HbS molecules polymerise into long rigid fibres
  -> red cell becomes sickle-shaped and stiff
  -> triggers: low oxygen, dehydration, acidosis, infection, cold
  -> repeated sickling damages the membrane -> irreversibly sickled cells
  -> (1) haemolysis: cells destroyed early (life span 10-20 days) -> anaemia, jaundice,
         gallstones
  -> (2) vaso-occlusion: sickled cells block small vessels -> ischaemia, pain crises,
         infarcts in bone, lungs (acute chest syndrome), spleen, brain (stroke)
```

**Features:** chronic haemolytic anaemia; painful crises in bones, chest and abdomen; hand-foot syndrome (swollen hands and feet in infants); repeated splenic infarcts shrink the spleen (autosplenectomy) → infections; leg ulcers; stroke; aplastic crisis with parvovirus B19. **Diagnosis:** sickling test, haemoglobin electrophoresis or HPLC showing HbS.

### Thalassaemia

**Aetiology:** inherited (autosomal recessive) disorders with reduced or absent synthesis of one type of globin chain: α-thalassaemia (α chains reduced; gene deletions) and β-thalassaemia (β chains reduced; point mutations). β-thalassaemia is a major health problem in India; carrier screening is advised before marriage or pregnancy.

**Pathogenesis (β-thalassaemia major):**

```text
Little or no beta chain -> less HbA -> microcytic hypochromic red cells
Excess free alpha chains precipitate inside red cell precursors
  -> damage membranes -> precursors die in marrow (ineffective erythropoiesis)
     and mature cells are destroyed in spleen (haemolysis) -> severe anaemia
Anaemia -> high erythropoietin -> massive marrow expansion
  -> bone deformity (frontal bossing, "hair-on-end" skull X-ray, prominent cheek bones)
  -> extramedullary haemopoiesis -> big liver and spleen
Increased iron absorption + repeated transfusions -> iron overload
  -> damage to heart, liver, endocrine glands (haemosiderosis)
```

**Forms:** β-thalassaemia major (homozygous; severe anaemia from about 6 months of age, needs regular transfusions), thalassaemia intermedia, and β-thalassaemia minor or trait (heterozygous; mild microcytosis, often no symptoms, raised HbA2). **Blood:** microcytic hypochromic cells, target cells, nucleated red cells; HbF raised in major.

### Hereditary and acquired haemolytic anaemias

**Haemolytic anaemia** results from early destruction of red cells (life span shorter than 120 days) faster than the marrow can replace them. Features: anaemia, jaundice (unconjugated bilirubin), dark urine, enlarged spleen, raised reticulocyte count, gallstones.

| Hereditary (defect inside the red cell) | Acquired (cause outside the red cell) |
| --- | --- |
| Membrane defects: hereditary spherocytosis (spectrin or ankyrin defect; small round fragile cells destroyed in the spleen) | Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (warm IgG or cold IgM antibodies against red cells) |
| Enzyme defects: G6PD deficiency (X-linked; red cells cannot withstand oxidant stress, so haemolysis follows some drugs such as primaquine, dapsone, sulphonamides, and fava beans or infection) | Drug-induced immune haemolysis; transfusion reactions; haemolytic disease of the newborn |
| Haemoglobin defects: sickle cell anaemia, thalassaemia | Mechanical damage (artificial heart valves), infections (malaria), burns, snake venom, hypersplenism |

### Haemophilia

**Definition:** an inherited bleeding disorder caused by deficiency of a clotting factor.

| Type | Missing factor | Inheritance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Haemophilia A (classic, commonest, about 80–85%) | Factor VIII | X-linked recessive |
| Haemophilia B (Christmas disease) | Factor IX | X-linked recessive |

Because the genes are on the X chromosome, males (one X) are affected and females are usually carriers; an affected father passes the gene to all daughters (carriers) and none of his sons.

**Pathogenesis:** lack of factor VIII or IX blocks the intrinsic pathway (the tenase complex), so thrombin and fibrin form too slowly; the platelet plug forms but is not stabilised, and bleeding restarts.

**Features:** severity depends on factor level. Bleeding into joints (haemarthrosis of knees, elbows, ankles) and muscles, often without injury in severe cases, leading to joint damage; prolonged bleeding after injury, tooth extraction or surgery; easy bruising. **Tests:** aPTT prolonged; PT, bleeding time and platelet count normal; low factor VIII or IX assay. Aspirin and intramuscular injections are avoided because they worsen bleeding.

## Remember

- ECF has Na⁺ and Cl⁻; ICF has K⁺; plasma is about 55% of blood.
- Albumin keeps fluid in vessels; low albumin causes oedema.
- Erythropoietin from the kidney drives red cell formation; B12 and folate are needed for DNA synthesis.
- Hb = 4 globin chains + 4 haem; HbA is α2β2.
- Extrinsic (VII, PT) and intrinsic (XII, XI, IX, VIII; aPTT) pathways meet at factor X → thrombin → fibrin.
- Vitamin K factors: II, VII, IX, X.
- O = universal donor, AB = universal recipient; anti-D prevents Rh disease of the newborn.
- Lymph returns about 3 L of fluid daily via the thoracic duct and right lymphatic duct.
- Inflammation: vascular events (dilatation, leakage) then cellular events (margination, rolling, adhesion, diapedesis, chemotaxis, phagocytosis).
- Iron deficiency = microcytic; B12/folate = megaloblastic; sickle cell = Glu6Val; thalassaemia = reduced globin chain; haemophilia A = factor VIII, X-linked.

# Unit 4: Peripheral nervous system and special senses with their disorders

The peripheral nervous system links the brain and spinal cord to the rest of the body. Its autonomic part controls the heart, glands and smooth muscle, which makes it the base of autonomic pharmacology. This unit covers the divisions of the peripheral nervous system, the sympathetic and parasympathetic systems, spinal and cranial nerves, the eye, ear, nose and tongue, and the common disorders of these special senses.

## 4.1 Organisation of the nervous system

```text
NERVOUS SYSTEM
 |-- Central nervous system (CNS): brain and spinal cord
 |-- Peripheral nervous system (PNS): cranial nerves (12 pairs), spinal nerves (31 pairs),
      ganglia and sensory receptors
        |-- Afferent (sensory) division: carries impulses from receptors to the CNS
        |      somatic sensory (skin, muscles, joints, special senses)
        |      visceral sensory (internal organs)
        |-- Efferent (motor) division: carries impulses from the CNS to effectors
               |-- Somatic nervous system: to skeletal muscle (voluntary);
               |      one neuron from CNS to muscle; transmitter acetylcholine
               |-- Autonomic nervous system (ANS): to cardiac muscle, smooth muscle
                      and glands (involuntary); two neurons in series
                      |-- Sympathetic division
                      |-- Parasympathetic division
                      |-- (Enteric nervous system: network in the gut wall)
```

## 4.2 Autonomic nervous system: general plan

Each autonomic pathway has two neurons: a **preganglionic neuron** with its cell body in the CNS and a myelinated axon (B fibre), and a **postganglionic neuron** with its cell body in an autonomic ganglion and an unmyelinated axon (C fibre) to the effector.

```text
CNS --- preganglionic neuron ---> [ganglion] --- postganglionic neuron ---> effector
         (releases ACh,                          (sympathetic: mostly noradrenaline;
          acts on nicotinic NN                     parasympathetic: ACh on
          receptors in ganglion)                   muscarinic receptors)
```

The adrenal medulla is a special case: preganglionic sympathetic fibres end directly on its chromaffin cells, which act like postganglionic neurons and release adrenaline (about 80%) and noradrenaline into blood.

### Comparison of sympathetic and parasympathetic divisions

| Feature | Sympathetic | Parasympathetic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Origin (outflow) | Thoracolumbar: lateral horn of spinal segments T1–L2 | Craniosacral: cranial nerves III, VII, IX, X and sacral segments S2–S4 |
| Ganglia | Close to the spinal cord: paravertebral sympathetic chain and prevertebral ganglia (coeliac, superior and inferior mesenteric) | Close to or inside the target organ (ciliary, pterygopalatine, submandibular, otic ganglia; intramural ganglia) |
| Preganglionic fibre | Short | Long |
| Postganglionic fibre | Long | Short |
| Ratio pre:post | One preganglionic neuron to many postganglionic neurons (widespread effect) | One to few (localised effect) |
| Transmitter at ganglion | Acetylcholine (nicotinic) | Acetylcholine (nicotinic) |
| Transmitter at effector | Noradrenaline (α and β adrenergic receptors); acetylcholine at sweat glands | Acetylcholine (muscarinic receptors) |
| General role | "Fight or flight": prepares for stress and exercise | "Rest and digest": saves and restores energy |

### Effects on organs

| Organ | Sympathetic | Parasympathetic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Eye – pupil | Dilates (mydriasis; radial muscle, α1) | Constricts (miosis; sphincter pupillae) |
| Eye – ciliary muscle | Relaxes slightly (far vision) | Contracts (near vision, accommodation) |
| Heart rate and force | Increased (β1) | Rate decreased (vagus) |
| Bronchi | Dilated (β2) | Constricted, more secretion |
| Blood vessels of skin and gut | Constricted (α1) | Little direct effect |
| Blood vessels of skeletal muscle | Dilated (β2) | — |
| Gut motility and secretion | Decreased; sphincters contracted | Increased; sphincters relaxed |
| Salivary glands | Thick scanty saliva | Profuse watery saliva |
| Urinary bladder | Detrusor relaxed, sphincter contracted (retention) | Detrusor contracted, sphincter relaxed (voiding) |
| Liver | Glycogen breakdown, glucose released | Glycogen formation |
| Sweat glands | Increased sweating (cholinergic sympathetic) | — |
| Adrenal medulla | Releases adrenaline | — |
| Male sex organs | Ejaculation | Erection |

Most organs have **dual innervation**, and the two divisions usually oppose each other. Some structures (most blood vessels, sweat glands, adrenal medulla) receive only sympathetic fibres.

## 4.3 Spinal nerves: origin and functions

There are **31 pairs** of spinal nerves: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral and 1 coccygeal. (There are 8 cervical nerves but 7 cervical vertebrae, because C1 leaves above the atlas.)

**Origin:** each spinal nerve is formed by two roots from one spinal segment:
- the **dorsal (posterior) root**, carrying sensory fibres, with the dorsal root ganglion containing the cell bodies of sensory neurons;
- the **ventral (anterior) root**, carrying motor fibres from cells in the anterior (and lateral) horn.

The two roots join in the intervertebral foramen to form a **mixed nerve** (sensory and motor). It then divides into a **dorsal ramus** (muscles and skin of the back), a **ventral ramus** (limbs and front and sides of the trunk), a meningeal branch, and rami communicantes (white and grey) that link with the sympathetic chain.

**Plexuses:** ventral rami (except T2–T12) join to form networks:

| Plexus | Roots | Main nerves and areas supplied |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cervical | C1–C4 | Skin and muscles of the neck; **phrenic nerve** (C3–C5) to the diaphragm |
| Brachial | C5–T1 | Upper limb: musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median and ulnar nerves |
| Lumbar | L1–L4 | Front and inner thigh: femoral and obturator nerves |
| Sacral | L4–S4 | Buttock, back of thigh, leg and foot: **sciatic nerve** (largest nerve of the body), pudendal nerve |

Thoracic ventral rami T2–T12 do not form plexuses; they run between the ribs as **intercostal nerves**.

**Dermatome:** an area of skin supplied by one spinal nerve. Dermatome maps help to locate spinal injuries; herpes zoster (shingles) produces a rash along a dermatome.

**Functions of spinal nerves:** carry sensations (touch, pain, temperature, position) from the body to the CNS, carry motor commands to skeletal muscles, carry autonomic fibres, and form the pathways for spinal reflexes (for example the knee jerk).

## 4.4 Cranial nerves: origin and functions

Twelve pairs arise from the brain (I from the cerebrum, II from the diencephalon, III–XII from the brainstem). A common memory aid for names: "Oh Oh Oh To Touch And Feel Very Good Velvet, Such Heaven"; and for type (S = sensory, M = motor, B = both): "Some Say Marry Money, But My Brother Says Big Brains Matter More".

| No. | Name | Origin (attachment) | Type | Main functions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| I | Olfactory | Olfactory bulb (cerebrum) | Sensory | Smell |
| II | Optic | Diencephalon (optic chiasma) | Sensory | Vision |
| III | Oculomotor | Midbrain | Motor (+ parasympathetic) | Moves eye (most extrinsic muscles), lifts upper eyelid, constricts pupil, accommodation |
| IV | Trochlear | Midbrain (back) | Motor | Superior oblique muscle (moves eye down and out) |
| V | Trigeminal | Pons | Mixed | Sensation of face, scalp, cornea, teeth (ophthalmic, maxillary, mandibular branches); muscles of chewing |
| VI | Abducens | Pons–medulla junction | Motor | Lateral rectus (moves eye outward) |
| VII | Facial | Pons–medulla junction | Mixed | Muscles of facial expression; taste from anterior two-thirds of tongue; tears and saliva (submandibular, sublingual glands) |
| VIII | Vestibulocochlear | Pons–medulla junction | Sensory | Hearing (cochlear) and balance (vestibular) |
| IX | Glossopharyngeal | Medulla | Mixed | Taste from posterior one-third of tongue; swallowing; parotid saliva; carotid sinus and body reflexes |
| X | Vagus | Medulla | Mixed | Parasympathetic supply to heart, lungs and gut; swallowing and speech muscles of pharynx and larynx; visceral sensation |
| XI | Accessory | Medulla and upper spinal cord | Motor | Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius (turning head, shrugging) |
| XII | Hypoglossal | Medulla | Motor | Muscles of the tongue |

**Clinical notes:** facial nerve palsy (Bell's palsy) causes drooping of one side of the face; trigeminal neuralgia causes severe facial pain; the vagus carries about three-quarters of all parasympathetic outflow.

## 4.5 Special senses: the eye

### Structure

```text
              conjunctiva
        cornea )  aqueous humour (anterior chamber)
   iris  ====( lens )====   ciliary body (ciliary muscle, suspensory ligaments)
        pupil      \
                    vitreous body (jelly in posterior cavity)
   Wall (outside to inside):
     Fibrous tunic:  sclera (white) + cornea (clear, front)
     Vascular tunic (uvea): choroid + ciliary body + iris
     Nervous tunic:  retina (rods and cones) -> optic disc (blind spot)
                     macula lutea with fovea centralis (sharpest vision)
   Optic nerve leaves at the back
```

| Part | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Cornea | Transparent front window; does most of the focusing (refraction); no blood vessels |
| Sclera | Tough white outer coat; protects and gives shape |
| Choroid | Blood vessels and pigment; nourishes the retina, absorbs stray light |
| Ciliary body | Ciliary muscle changes lens shape (accommodation); ciliary processes secrete aqueous humour |
| Iris | Coloured part; sphincter (parasympathetic) and dilator (sympathetic) muscles control pupil size |
| Lens | Transparent, elastic, biconvex; fine focusing |
| Aqueous humour | Fluid in front of the lens; nourishes lens and cornea; maintains intraocular pressure (about 10–21 mm Hg) |
| Vitreous body | Gel that keeps the eyeball's shape and holds the retina in place |
| Retina | Rods (dim light, black-and-white vision; pigment rhodopsin needs vitamin A) and cones (bright light, colour, sharp vision; most dense in the fovea) |

**Accessory structures:** eyelids, eyelashes, eyebrows, conjunctiva, lacrimal apparatus (lacrimal gland → tears → lacrimal puncta → lacrimal sac → nasolacrimal duct → nose; this is why eye drops can be tasted), and six extrinsic muscles (four recti, two obliques).

### Physiology of vision

Light passes through cornea → aqueous humour → pupil → lens → vitreous → retina. The image is refracted and focused upside down on the retina. **Accommodation** for near objects: ciliary muscle contracts → suspensory ligaments slacken → lens becomes rounder; pupils constrict and eyes converge. In the retina, light changes rhodopsin, producing signals that pass through bipolar and ganglion cells to the optic nerve, optic chiasma (where fibres from the nasal half of each retina cross), optic tract, lateral geniculate body and visual cortex in the occipital lobe.

## 4.6 Special senses: the ear

```text
EXTERNAL EAR        MIDDLE EAR (air-filled)          INNER EAR (fluid-filled, temporal bone)
auricle (pinna)     tympanic membrane                bony labyrinth with perilymph,
external acoustic   ossicles: malleus -> incus ->    membranous labyrinth with endolymph:
meatus (wax glands)           stapes -> oval window    - cochlea (hearing; organ of Corti)
                    auditory (Eustachian) tube          - vestibule (utricle, saccule)
                    to nasopharynx                      - semicircular canals (3)
```

| Part | Function |
| --- | --- |
| Auricle and canal | Collect and direct sound; wax (cerumen) traps dust and protects |
| Tympanic membrane | Vibrates with sound waves |
| Ossicles | Carry and amplify vibrations to the oval window |
| Eustachian tube | Equalises air pressure on both sides of the eardrum; drains the middle ear |
| Cochlea (organ of Corti) | Hair cells convert vibrations into nerve impulses (hearing) |
| Utricle and saccule | Static balance and linear acceleration (otoliths) |
| Semicircular canals | Dynamic balance: rotational movements of the head |

**Physiology of hearing:** sound waves → eardrum vibrates → ossicles → oval window → pressure waves in perilymph and endolymph → basilar membrane moves → hair cells bend against the tectorial membrane → nerve impulses in the cochlear nerve → auditory cortex in the temporal lobe. High-pitched sounds stimulate the base of the cochlea, low-pitched sounds the apex.

## 4.7 Special senses: the nose (smell)

The **olfactory epithelium** lies in the roof of the nasal cavity. It contains olfactory receptor cells (bipolar neurons with cilia carrying odour receptors), supporting cells and basal stem cells; olfactory receptor neurons are replaced throughout life. Odour molecules dissolve in mucus and bind receptors (G-protein coupled) → impulses pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone along the olfactory nerve → olfactory bulb → olfactory tract → olfactory cortex in the temporal lobe and limbic system (hence the link between smell, emotion and memory). Smell adapts quickly and contributes much of what we call "flavour".

**Other functions of the nose:** passage for air, warming, moistening and filtering of inspired air (hairs, mucus, cilia), resonance of the voice, and drainage of the paranasal sinuses and tears. Its rich blood supply is used for nasal drug delivery.

## 4.8 Special senses: the tongue (taste)

**Taste buds** lie mainly on the papillae of the tongue (circumvallate papillae at the back, fungiform at the tip and sides, foliate on the sides; filiform papillae have no taste buds and give a rough surface), and also on the soft palate and pharynx. Each taste bud has gustatory (receptor) cells with microvilli projecting into a taste pore, supporting cells and basal cells; receptor cells are replaced about every 10 days.

**Basic tastes:** sweet, salty, sour, bitter and umami (savoury, glutamate). The old "tongue map" with strict zones is not accurate; all tastes can be sensed over most of the tongue.

**Pathway:** facial nerve (VII, anterior two-thirds), glossopharyngeal nerve (IX, posterior one-third), vagus nerve (X, throat and epiglottis) → medulla → thalamus → gustatory cortex. **Other functions of the tongue:** chewing, mixing food with saliva, swallowing, speech, and the sublingual route for drug absorption.

## 4.9 Pathophysiology of special sense disorders

### Glaucoma

**Definition:** a group of eye diseases with damage to the optic nerve and loss of visual field, usually associated with raised intraocular pressure (IOP). It is a leading cause of irreversible blindness.

**Normal flow of aqueous humour:**

```text
Ciliary processes secrete aqueous -> posterior chamber -> through pupil
 -> anterior chamber -> angle between iris and cornea
 -> trabecular meshwork -> canal of Schlemm -> veins
 (smaller uveoscleral route through the ciliary muscle)
```

**Pathogenesis:** when outflow is blocked, aqueous builds up and IOP rises (usually above 21 mm Hg). High pressure compresses the axons and blood supply of the optic nerve head → ganglion cell death → "cupping" of the optic disc → loss of peripheral vision first, then central vision.

| Type | Mechanism | Features |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Primary open-angle glaucoma** (commonest) | Angle is open but the trabecular meshwork resists outflow | Slow, painless, no early symptoms; gradual loss of side vision ("tunnel vision"); detected by screening |
| **Primary angle-closure glaucoma** | Iris is pushed forward and blocks the angle (narrow angles, hypermetropic eyes); can be triggered by pupil dilatation (dim light, anticholinergic drugs) | Acute attack: sudden severe eye pain, red eye, blurred vision, haloes around lights, headache, nausea and vomiting; an emergency |
| **Secondary glaucoma** | Due to another cause: long-term corticosteroids, uveitis, injury, swollen cataract | |
| **Congenital glaucoma** | Developmental defect of the angle | Large eyes in infants (buphthalmos), watering, light sensitivity |

**Risk factors:** age over 40, family history, myopia (open-angle), hypermetropia (angle-closure), diabetes, steroid use.

### Cataract

**Definition:** opacity (loss of transparency) of the lens, causing blurred vision. It is the commonest cause of curable blindness in India.

**Aetiology:** ageing (senile cataract, the commonest), diabetes, long-term corticosteroids, ultraviolet light, smoking, eye injury, inflammation (uveitis), radiation, and congenital cataract (rubella in pregnancy, galactosaemia).

**Pathogenesis:** the lens is made of long fibre cells packed with ordered crystallin proteins. With age and oxidative stress, crystallins are oxidised, cross-linked and aggregated; the lens loses antioxidant glutathione, water and ion balance are disturbed, and the proteins clump and scatter light. In diabetes, excess glucose in the lens is converted by aldose reductase into sorbitol, which draws in water and makes fibres swell and become opaque.

**Features:** gradual painless blurring of vision, glare and haloes at night, faded colours, frequent change of glasses, and a white or grey pupil in advanced cases. Treatment is surgical replacement with an intraocular lens.

### Myopia (short-sightedness)

**Definition:** a refractive error in which parallel rays of light are focused **in front of** the retina when the eye is at rest, so distant objects look blurred while near objects are clear.

**Cause:** an eyeball that is too long (axial myopia, commonest) or a cornea or lens with too much refractive power (refractive myopia). Genetic tendency and prolonged near work with little time outdoors increase the risk; it often starts in school-age children and progresses during growth.

```text
Normal eye:  rays -> (lens) -> focus ON retina
Myopic eye:  rays -> (lens) -> focus IN FRONT of retina -> blurred image
Correction:  concave (diverging, minus) lens moves the focus back onto the retina
```

High myopia stretches the retina and raises the risk of retinal detachment and glaucoma. (For comparison: hypermetropia focuses behind the retina and is corrected by a convex lens; presbyopia is age-related loss of accommodation.)

### Otitis externa

**Definition:** inflammation of the external ear canal.

**Aetiology:** bacteria (mostly *Pseudomonas aeruginosa* and *Staphylococcus aureus*) and fungi (*Aspergillus*, *Candida*). Predisposing factors: moisture from swimming ("swimmer's ear") and humidity, which wash away protective wax; injury from cotton buds or fingernails; skin conditions (eczema); hearing aids.

**Pathogenesis:** loss of the acidic, water-repelling wax layer and damage to the thin canal skin let microbes enter → inflammation and swelling of the canal.

**Features:** ear pain made worse by pulling the pinna or pressing the tragus, itching, discharge, swelling of the canal, and muffled hearing. Malignant (necrotising) otitis externa is a severe spreading infection in elderly diabetics.

### Otitis media

**Definition:** inflammation of the middle ear; common in children.

**Aetiology:** usually follows a cold or upper respiratory infection. Bacteria: *Streptococcus pneumoniae*, *Haemophilus influenzae*, *Moraxella catarrhalis*; also viruses. Children are prone because their Eustachian tube is shorter, wider and more horizontal; enlarged adenoids, bottle feeding while lying down and passive smoking add to the risk.

**Pathogenesis:**

```text
Upper respiratory infection -> swelling of the Eustachian tube lining
 -> tube blocked -> air absorbed, negative pressure in middle ear
 -> fluid collects (effusion); microbes from nasopharynx multiply in it
 -> pus forms, pressure rises -> bulging red eardrum, pain, fever
 -> may perforate -> discharge (relieves pain)
```

**Types and features:** acute otitis media (earache, fever, irritability, pulling at the ear in infants, reduced hearing, bulging drum); otitis media with effusion ("glue ear", fluid without infection, hearing loss); chronic suppurative otitis media (long-standing perforation with discharge). Complications: hearing loss, mastoiditis, meningitis.

### Vertigo

**Definition:** a false sensation that oneself or the surroundings are spinning or moving. It is a symptom, usually of a disorder of the vestibular system.

| Type | Causes |
| --- | --- |
| **Peripheral** (inner ear or vestibular nerve; commoner) | **Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo** (BPPV: loose otoconia crystals move into a semicircular canal, so turning the head triggers brief spinning); **Ménière's disease** (excess endolymph – endolymphatic hydrops – causing attacks of vertigo with hearing loss, tinnitus and fullness in the ear); **vestibular neuritis** (viral inflammation of the vestibular nerve); labyrinthitis; motion sickness |
| **Central** (brainstem or cerebellum) | Stroke, multiple sclerosis, tumours, migraine |

**Pathophysiology:** balance depends on matching signals from both vestibular organs, the eyes and joint receptors. When one side sends an abnormal signal, the brain senses movement that is not happening. **Features:** spinning sensation, nausea and vomiting, sweating, unsteadiness, and nystagmus (jerky eye movements). Some drugs (aminoglycoside antibiotics) can damage the vestibular apparatus.

### Anosmia

**Definition:** complete loss of the sense of smell (hyposmia = reduced smell).

**Aetiology and pathogenesis:**

| Type | Causes |
| --- | --- |
| Conductive (odours cannot reach the receptors) | Common cold, allergic rhinitis, sinusitis, nasal polyps, deviated nasal septum, tumours |
| Sensorineural (receptors or nerve pathway damaged) | Viral infections (including COVID-19, which damages supporting cells of the olfactory epithelium), head injury shearing the olfactory nerve fibres at the cribriform plate, ageing, neurodegenerative diseases (Parkinson's, Alzheimer's), brain tumours, smoking, toxins and some drugs, congenital (Kallmann syndrome) |

**Effects:** reduced flavour of food and loss of appetite, inability to detect smoke, gas leaks or spoiled food, and depression.

## Remember

- PNS = 12 cranial + 31 spinal nerve pairs; efferent PNS = somatic + autonomic.
- Sympathetic: T1–L2, short pre/long post, noradrenaline; parasympathetic: III, VII, IX, X and S2–S4, long pre/short post, acetylcholine.
- All autonomic ganglia use acetylcholine on nicotinic receptors; sweat glands are sympathetic but cholinergic.
- Spinal nerve: dorsal root sensory (with ganglion), ventral root motor; plexuses cervical, brachial, lumbar, sacral.
- Cranial nerves: I smell, II vision, III/IV/VI eye movements, V face sensation and chewing, VII face muscles and taste, VIII hearing and balance, IX/X swallowing and viscera, XI neck, XII tongue.
- Aqueous humour drains through trabecular meshwork and canal of Schlemm; blockage → glaucoma.
- Cataract = lens opacity (crystallin aggregation, sorbitol in diabetes); myopia = focus in front of retina, concave lens.
- Otitis externa = canal (Pseudomonas, swimmer's ear); otitis media = middle ear after Eustachian tube blockage, common in children.
- Vertigo is a spinning illusion (BPPV, Ménière's, vestibular neuritis); anosmia is loss of smell (conductive or sensorineural).
